If the goal is to adapt similar mechanisms to training-time multimodal conditioning, spend more time on memory construction, retrieval overhead, and the exact fusion design.3d:T41d,SSDi8 combines execution-path engineering with SSD-aware quantization:
- Persistent INT8 path: identify channel-/shape-varying activations that are repeatedly reused across SSD modules; quantize them at carefully chosen points and reuse cached INT8 activations to avoid frequent precision bouncing and DRAM overhead.
- Element-wise/GEMM entanglement: SSD interleaves element-wise multiplications with matrix multiplications, which commonly forces higher-precision intermediates. The paper proposes a sparse-aware reformulation that reorganizes these computations so INT8 kernels can be used end-to-end, and argues correctness via a formal equivalence analysis.
- Exploit SSD’s intrinsic 2D structure: the external model dimension is effectively factored into (num_heads, head_dim) with different outlier behaviors; SSDi8 explicitly leverages this to reduce quantization error instead of using a single coarse scaling scheme.
- Error-mean correction: add a per-channel error-mean correction term to compensate systematic bias and improve PTQ stability.3e:T4bf,All models are GPT-2 scale: 12 layers, 12 heads, hidden size 768, trained for 3 epochs on a 1B-token OpenWebText split, for roughly 3B token exposures. As dense language models, softmax variants remain better: sigmoid is worse by about 0.36 PPL with RoPE and about 1.21 PPL without RoPE. The picture changes once learned hard eviction is introduced. Relative to their own no-eviction references, the sigmoid-gated models achieve useful deletion rates with almost no perplexity cost. Sig+G RoPE removes 19.8% of KV entries with essentially unchanged PPL (22.424 vs 22.440), and Sig+G NoPE removes 32.2% with only a small increase (24.637 vs 24.603). Under a matched live-cache protocol, the learned sigmoid-gated models also outperform the paper’s H2O and KeyDiff implementations, whereas softmax-gated models do not. A random support-removal probe is important here: sigmoid attention is not generically more robust to arbitrary KV deletion, and can in fact be more sensitive than softmax at larger random removal rates. That strengthens the paper’s interpretation that the gain comes from better compatibility between learned deletion patterns and the attention substrate, not from generic deletion robustness.3f:T652,The methodology rests on three intentionally independent measurement paths. First, the authors build a 64-shape sweep of LLM primitives that preserve semantics while changing expression form, and they record supported-device sets per operation rather than a vague residency score. This is how they establish that placement is a property of expression, not semantics. A representative example is that fused RMSNorm is fully eligible while an equivalent subln decomposition is not admitted to ANE execution. Second, they train matched real models across architecture families, sizes, and precisions. Quantized checkpoints are byte-identical in structure to their fp16 counterparts, so deployment comparisons isolate encoding rather than graph differences. Third, they read ANE memory-controller byte counters during inference, which lets them verify what actually ran and how many bytes were moved, instead of trusting compile-time plans or fragile power telemetry. From these measurements they derive several mechanism-level conclusions. Placement is jointly determined by architecture, size, and encoding rather than parameter count alone. Once resident, decode behaves like streaming the full weight set every token, so latency is largely a function of bytes streamed per token. They also show that heavily grouped GQA, especially with 2 KV heads, is a smaller and more compiler-friendly operator family on ANE than the conv-heavy alternatives examined. This reverses the usual CPU-side intuition: on this accelerator, the advantage comes from grouping and byte economy, not from an abstract preference for attention.40:T5ff,Several results carry most of the paper’s weight. On placement, semantically equivalent formulations can diverge completely: fused RMSNorm is reported as 100% eligible while the decomposed form is 0%, which directly supports the expression-vs-semantics claim. On architecture and encoding, a 22.3M attention model in fp16 runs on ANE, while a 25.9M conv-heavy fp16 model does not; yet the same conv graph in int8 or 2-bit reaches roughly 83% on-ANE residency. This shows that parameter count is not the governing variable. On decode cost, hardware counters measure about 1.539 / 0.753 / 0.197 bytes per parameter for fp16 / int8 / 2-bit, versus nominal 2 / 1 / 0.25, indicating real-system packing and runtime effects but confirming that streamed weight bytes dominate. On operator size, heavily grouped GQA with 2 KV heads is around 2.5d^2, whereas the LIV conv family is around 4d^2, and the grouped-attention family is admitted at fp16 while the conv-heavy family is the one that falls off ANE. On the end-to-end frontier, ternary models occupy the best size/speed tradeoff among the tested artifacts: around 25M ternary models span roughly 10.0–10.8 MB and 0.62–0.64 ms across operator mixes, while 50M ternary models are about 16.8 MB and 0.86 ms. Relative to the conv-heavy fp16 starting point, the reported gains are 9.8×/6.1× smaller and 3.0×/2.2× faster. An important secondary observation is that once encoding is pushed to ternary, operator mix matters much less for size and speed than the encoding choice itself.41:T4e9,Read this paper as an evidence chain rather than a benchmark story. Start with the introduction and Table 1 to fix the five headline claims. Then go to §4.1 first: the primitive sweep is the cleanest part of the paper and the best place to understand why the authors insist that expression form, not semantic equivalence, controls placement. Next read §5.1 and §5.2 together. §5.1 explains why matched trained artifacts matter; §5.2 explains why runtime byte counters are necessary and how cross-chip telemetry calibration can fail silently. After that, focus on §6–§8, which map to placement, bytes-per-token, and the operator lever. The figures showing architecture × size × encoding interactions and the relationship between bytes/param and latency are the ones to study carefully. If time is limited, keep two questions in mind: why does the paper recommend choosing encoding before parameter budget, and why does grouped attention become the smaller operator family on ANE. The deeper follow-up questions are whether compiler-admissible graph forms can be enforced during training, whether byte-dominated decode should change how low-bit models are pretrained, and how much of this transfers to other NPUs rather than remaining ANE-specific.42:T5f0,The central idea is predictive delta prefetching. First, the system predicts downstream sparsity early. Instead of using per-layer predictors that reveal a layer’s active set only when execution reaches that layer, NeuroPrefetcher runs a single GPU-resident predictor after layer 0 and predicts active-neuron masks for all downstream MLP layers in one shot from early-token features. This creates a lookahead I/O schedule before sparse execution begins. Second, the runtime converts predictions into movement decisions. For each layer it tracks which weight rows are already resident, compares that resident set with the predicted active set for the next token, and fetches only the incoming delta from NVMe. This reframes the I/O cost from “how many rows are needed now” to “how many new rows are needed relative to the previous token.” Third, the implementation addresses a platform-specific coherence issue on Jetson-style unified-memory systems: direct I/O can bypass CPU cache coherence and expose stale data to the GPU, so sparse rows are routed through a cache-coherent staging path before execution. Fourth, the runtime uses a memory-adaptive dense/sparse split. Limited GPU memory is divided between a fully resident dense prefix and a sparse suffix with active-row buffers. With more memory, more early layers stay dense; with less memory, the sparse suffix expands to preserve model executability. The design is therefore not just sparse execution, but a coordinated predictor-runtime-memory policy.43:T4fd,The most important evidence starts with system profiling. On a Jetson AGX Orin running Mistral-7B with a 14G memory setting, decoding triggers about 11,453 major page faults per second; the CPU spends 77% of its time blocked on I/O, while the GPU averages only 3% utilization. This establishes that the bottleneck is reactive weight movement rather than arithmetic throughput. The enabling observation is also quantified clearly: around 82–85% of active MLP neurons persist across adjacent tokens. The experimental story appears to have three main parts: predictor quality and lookahead timing; end-to-end gains of delta prefetching over demand paging and prior sparse runtimes; and the trade-off induced by the dense/sparse split under different memory budgets. The introduction names relevant baselines such as llama.cpp with mmap plus demand paging, PowerInfer, LLM in a Flash, and Neuralink-style placement ideas. For a reader, the most useful results are likely not a single average speedup number, but the breakdowns showing reduced page faults, lower I/O stall time, smaller NVMe traffic, better GPU utilization, and improved decode latency. The provided full-text excerpt does not include the final result tables, so it would be unsafe to invent exact speedup values.44:T50f,Geodesia-KV is a training-free family of cache policies. It partitions the cache into 64-token blocks and assigns each block to a monotone precision ladder: exact 16-bit storage, 8/4/2-bit scalar quantization, or a 1-bit centroid-like representation. Block importance is tracked through a causal EMA of observed attention mass, so allocation decisions depend only on the prefix. For GQA models, allocation is performed once per physical KV head by aggregating masses across the associated query heads.

The allocator is framed as a monotone rate-distortion problem. After a block leaves the recent window, it may be demoted but not promoted, since the dense copy is no longer kept. This design makes in-place compression possible and prevents hidden memory costs from a fallback representation. The bit depth is selected from attention mass and a reconstruction-error proxy: blocks with high attention mass or larger distortion risk receive more bits. The method also adds exact residuals for a small set of high-impact tokens, selected from prompt attention mass and value reconstruction error. The Compressed-Quest variant combines query-sparse page reading with compressed resident pages: exact key boxes are used for page ranking, while resident K/V tensors follow the graded representation.45:T42f,The experiments cover 3B and 8B checkpoints, with long-context evaluations on WikiText-2 and PG-19. A central experimental point is the causal Q=1 setup and separate accounting of resident and read rates. The authors show that chunked teacher forcing can alter the reported rate of a method such as KIVI; in their implementation, KIVI changes from about 5.03 bits/value with a 64-token chunk to about 5.69 bits/value with a 1024-token chunk.

On WikiText-2 with a 16k context, the 5-bit operating point of Geodesia-KV achieves lower perplexity at a lower bitrate than KIVI-4 on Qwen. The Compressed-Quest version improves perplexity while reducing resident cost, with a reported comparison of 9.83 versus 16.25 bits/value. The PG-19 study uses a preregistered window list and cluster bootstrap intervals to separate robust effects from small-window artifacts. The paper also reports native vLLM integration and practical resident-capacity gains on GQA and MLA models, along with several negative results for spectral, quantum-inspired, VQ, and static-protection variants.46:T85b,方法上有三个关键设计。其一是 extractive compression：模型不是重写代码和工具输出，而是从输入段落中选择要保留的 span，并配合一组固定的结构标记表示删除区域。这样做的目的很明确，不是追求语言自然，而是尽量保证 identifier、path、number、error string 这类 downstream edit 依赖的精确字符串不被改坏。文中对这一点做了审计，训练语料上 96.0% 的 identifier/path/number 来自输入拷贝，held-out SWE-bench Lite 上是 96.2%；如果排除作者刻意允许改写的一类对象，这个比例到 98.3%。

其二是 intent conditioning。每次压缩不是只看 segment 本身，而是同时输入当前任务 query，让模型优先保留 query 中点名的实体、文件、函数、报错线索。作者强调“什么重要”不是静态属性，而是相对当前 agent 目标定义的，这也是它和通用压缩器的主要区别。

其三是 pipeline 设计。系统先做 segmentation、kind classification 和 level labeling，再按 segment 单独压缩。压缩模型只看到 task + 单个 segment + kind/level tag，不直接接收数值 token budget；预算通过 system prompt 中的 level-to-ratio 表间接传达。作者原本设计了四级重要性标签 L0-L3，并希望不同 level 对应不同压缩率，但实验发现蒸馏后的 student 实际只学出了两个有效压缩带宽，四级设计没有按预期落地。这个负结果作者没有回避，反而是全文里比较有价值的部分。

数据方面，作者从 67,074 条 OpenHands 轨迹出发，经过五阶段流水线，构建出 45K segment distillation pool 和 40,606 条 teacher-validated compression examples，带有 intent-conditioned target、level label 和 must-keep annotation。训练上比较了三个匹配 backbone，最后选 4B；还尝试过对 drop supervision 加权，但结果适得其反，最终部署版本没有采用。更有意思的是，最终上线 checkpoint 不是训练 loss 最优，而是通过 OOD sweep 选出来的，说明这个任务里 loss 和真实可用性并不严格一致。47:T89d,The method has three main pieces. First, it uses extractive compression. Instead of rewriting code and tool outputs, the model selects spans from the input and uses a fixed set of structural markers to denote removed regions. The reason is straightforward: downstream edits depend on exact strings, so identifiers, paths, numbers, and error messages should be copied, not paraphrased. The paper audits this claim explicitly: 96.0% of emitted identifier/path/number-like tokens are copied from the input on the training corpus, and 96.2% on held-out SWE-bench Lite outputs; excluding the one category intentionally rewritten by design, the rate reaches 98.3%.

Second, the compressor is intent-conditioned. Each compression call receives both the current task/query and a single segment, so the model can prioritize entities, files, functions, and error clues named in the live task. The paper argues that importance is not intrinsic to a segment; it is defined relative to what the agent is trying to do now.

Third, the system is built as a pipeline. A gateway performs segmentation, kind classification, and level labeling, and the model compresses one segment at a time. The compressor sees the task plus one segment with kind/level tags, but no explicit numeric token budget. Budget control is only indirectly encoded through a static level-to-ratio table in the system prompt. The authors originally designed four importance levels, L0-L3, but report that the distilled student effectively learned only two usable compression bands. That negative result is one of the more informative parts of the paper.

On data, they start from 67,074 raw OpenHands trajectories and build a five-stage pipeline that yields a 45K-segment distillation pool and 40,606 teacher-validated compression examples with intent-conditioned targets, level labels, and must-keep annotations. On training, they compare three matched backbones and choose 4B. They also tried drop-supervision weighting, found that it backfired, and shipped without it. Notably, the deployed checkpoint was selected by an out-of-distribution sweep rather than by training loss, which suggests that lower loss did not reliably predict real utility.48:T53a,The evaluation has two layers. The intrinsic evaluation focuses on OOD holdout performance, including compression quality, must-keep retention, and identifier retention, with confidence intervals. One notable result is that at comparable budgets, the student does not underperform its own teacher on must-keep identifier retention, which suggests that distillation preserved the key exact-copy behavior.

The end-to-end evaluation plugs Paritok-4B into a coding-agent workflow under both raw-source and in-distribution line-numbered settings. The headline result is a 25.7% compression rate, meaning roughly one quarter of the original context is retained, while maintaining comparable single-shot solve quality. The paper describes this as roughly twice as aggressive as strong GPT-based compressors. Interestingly, the expected trade-off did not appear in the predicted form: instead of harder compression at equal quality, they observed slightly softer compression with higher quality, and no paired degradation was statistically resolvable over 300 instances.

That said, the scope is narrow. The conclusions are tied to coding-agent trajectories, the specific segmentation pipeline, and teacher-generated targets. The collapse from four intended levels to two effective bands also shows that fine-grained budget control remains weak.49:T6d8,The method organizes each logical KV page into a three-tier lifecycle: Recent, Anchor, and Stale. Recent and Anchor pages are stored in FP8, while Stale pages are stored in a 3-bit TQ3 format. Recent covers fresh tokens needed for local coherence and ongoing reasoning. Anchor is reserved for globally important regions such as system prompts, attention sinks, retrieved evidence, or structural headers. Stale holds older non-anchor content that should not be dropped. The key contribution is not merely mixed precision, but integrating mixed precision into the paged-attention runtime itself. Every live-request page remains addressable; pages are not evicted. Format-specific kernels compute partial attention statistics on different physical formats, and the outputs are merged through a stable global softmax merge, instead of reconstructing a unified dense cache first. The paper also keeps key/value asymmetry explicit: key distortion changes routing, while value distortion changes retrieved content, so the codec and kernel interfaces preserve separate treatment for K and V even if a deployment uses the same nominal tier for both. The controller uses page age, structural metadata, attention statistics, layer/head sensitivity, K/V role, and current memory pressure to decide transitions. Attention-based promotion is built on globally normalized page mass, not raw local scores, so pages from different physical partitions remain comparable. On the engineering side, the paper adds an ownership protocol, fallback paths, dense-shadow and physical-byte instrumentation, and a CUDA-graph-compatible heterogeneous decode path. That makes the contribution primarily a runtime integration story rather than a new compression formula in isolation.4a:T5fa,The main evaluation is on Qwen3.6-27B using a single 96GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU. The paper first explains the compression opportunity from the model structure: Qwen3.6-27B has 64 language layers arranged as 16 groups of three Gated DeltaNet layers followed by one full-attention layer, so only 16 layers contribute attention KV. Each such layer has 4 KV heads with head dimension 256. Under this setup, the theoretical BF16 attention-cache cost is exactly 2.00 GiB per 32K-token sequence and 8.00 GiB per 128K-token sequence. Minima-KV reports 18.3 KiB of attention KV per live token in deployment accounting, which is a 3.50x reduction relative to BF16 and a 1.75x reduction relative to FP8. On quality, the paper reports profile-separated evidence. The clearly stated results include parity with the dense control on 16K RULER NIAH, less than 1% regression on 4K RULER NIAH, and LongBench v2 evaluation up to 64K context. One important caveat is highlighted by the authors: Qwen3.6 also has a separate per-sequence Gated DeltaNet recurrent state, which is not counted as compressed attention KV. That means the concurrency gain from KV compression is bounded by other fixed per-sequence allocations. This is an important systems point, because raw KV compression ratio does not translate directly into throughput gain. From the available full text, the evaluation is more deployment- and quality-oriented than analytically broad; there is limited evidence of cross-family validation or deeper generalization studies.4b:T416,For a quick read, focus on three parts. First, read the Introduction and Background to understand that the paper is not just about quantization; it is about retention-preserving lifecycle management for KV pages. Those are the most informative technical pieces. Two deeper questions are worth following up: whether the page-level normalized attention mass is stable enough as a control signal, and whether this kind of runtime hierarchy could eventually influence training-time long-range dependency modeling.4c:T87f,方法分三步：generation、routing、refinement。先从同一个生成模型独立采样 n 条完整轨迹，再用 reward model 对整条轨迹打分。与直接按绝对分数阈值决策不同，SRD 采用 rank-normalized score，把候选按 reward 排序后映射到 [0,1] 区间，再用两个阈值 θ_low 和 θ_high 做三路路由：高分样本 Keep，中间样本 Refine，低分样本 Discard。这样做的动机是减少不同题目、不同 reward 尺度下绝对分数不稳定的问题。

真正的创新在 refinement。对进入 Refine 的边界样本，算法不会整条重采，而是沿轨迹按固定步长 m 检查 prefix-level reward 变化，寻找最早出现“相对前缀退化”的位置 j，把 j 之后的 suffix 截掉并重新生成。重生成时提高采样温度，目的是增加局部探索，避免原轨迹在同一错误模式附近反复采样。新 suffix 接回原 prefix 后，再重新打分并与其他活跃候选一起排序，只保留最终进入 Keep 的样本。

论文还给了理论分析。核心结论是，在温和假设下，SRD 相比 rejection sampling 有严格更高的期望最优轨迹质量，并带来约 1.28–1.36 倍的 sample efficiency 提升，且收益会随候选池增大而上升。文中把收益写成与 (1 + ρ·p_M/p_H) 相关的形式，其中 p_M、p_H 对应中等质量可修复样本与高质量样本的概率质量，ρ 则刻画 refinement 成功率。这个表达很重要，因为它说明 SRD 不是无条件占优：只有当“边界样本里确实存在可救前缀”且 reward 能识别退化位置时，局部重写才有意义。

和已有方法相比，Best-of-N 只会在末端选择，完全不回收中间结构；speculative rejection 会更早停掉低质前缀，但一旦拒绝就不可逆；Controlled Decoding 依赖 prefix-aware value function 在 token 级引导，而 SRD 不需要额外训练 value function，也不需要更大 teacher，只需生成模型加 reward model。代价是它仍然依赖完整轨迹采样和额外 reward 评估，且边界定位目前较粗，主要靠固定间隔扫描，不是细粒度 token-level attribution。4d:T95d,SRD has three stages: generation, routing, and refinement. It first samples n complete trajectories from the same generator, then scores them with a reward model. Instead of using an absolute reward threshold, it converts rewards into rank-normalized scores in [0,1], and applies two thresholds, theta_low and theta_high, to route candidates into Keep, Refine, or Discard. The motivation is practical: absolute reward scales are often unstable across tasks and prompts, while rank is more robust.

The main novelty is the refinement stage. For borderline candidates routed to Refine, SRD does not resample the whole trajectory. It scans the trajectory at fixed intervals m, evaluates prefix-level reward behavior, and finds the earliest point j where quality appears to degrade relative to the preceding prefix. It then truncates the suffix after j and regenerates only that suffix, using a higher sampling temperature to encourage local exploration and avoid repeating the same failure mode. The repaired trajectory is rescored and reranked jointly with the remaining candidates, and is kept only if it survives the final routing.

The paper also provides a theoretical analysis. Under mild assumptions, SRD achieves strictly higher expected best-trajectory quality than rejection sampling and improves sample efficiency by about 1.28–1.36x, with gains increasing as the candidate pool grows. The gain is characterized by a term of the form (1 + rho * p_M / p_H), where p_M and p_H capture the mass of repairable medium-quality samples and already-high-quality samples, and rho reflects refinement success. This matters because it clarifies when SRD should help: only when there is a meaningful population of salvageable trajectories and the reward signal can identify degradation reliably.

Relative to prior work, best-of-N only selects at the end and never recovers partial structure; speculative rejection can stop early but is irreversible once a prefix is rejected; Controlled Decoding uses a learned prefix-aware value function for token-level steering, whereas SRD needs only a generator and a reward model, with no larger teacher and no separately trained value function. The trade-off is that SRD still requires full-trajectory sampling up front and extra reward evaluations, and its boundary detection is fairly coarse, based on interval scanning rather than token-level attribution.4e:T6b0,The experiments cover MATH500, GPQA, HotpotQA, and AlpacaEval, spanning mathematical reasoning, science QA, multi-hop QA, and instruction following. The main empirical claim is about the accuracy-compute frontier rather than a single accuracy number: at matched or near-matched quality, SRD uses fewer generated tokens; under low compute budgets, it tends to outperform speculative rejection; under larger budgets, it approaches best-of-N quality at lower cost.

The clearest number stated in the paper is the theoretical 1.28–1.36x sample-efficiency gain. The full text indicates that the gain becomes more visible with larger candidate pools, because more borderline trajectories become available for repair. The ablations focus on two issues. First, reward calibration: when rewards are stable and ranking is reliable, conservative global rerouting works better because it identifies worthwhile candidates more consistently; when rewards are noisy, local self-comparison is more robust because it reduces misrouting from cross-sample score instability. Second, refinement boundary choice: truncating too early destroys useful context, while truncating too late leaves too little room for repair, so the interval size m and routing thresholds matter.

A useful experimental detail is that the authors test multiple generator–reward model pairings rather than tying the method to one specific model stack. That suggests SRD is a search-layer improvement rather than an artifact of a single base model. Still, many results are presented as tradeoff curves and relative gains, so readers who care about exact token costs and absolute per-benchmark deltas should inspect the main tables and appendix carefully.4f:T5a4,For a quick read, start with the introduction and the main method figure. The key idea is simple: SRD does not just sample more trajectories and pick one; it repairs near-miss trajectories by preserving good prefixes. Then read the routing rule and the regeneration-boundary definition. The use of rank-normalized reward, rather than absolute reward, is an important design choice because it determines how stable the method is across tasks.

After that, skim the theory section for the main proposition rather than every proof detail. Focus on the assumptions behind the sample-efficiency gain: the prevalence of repairable borderline samples, the success rate of suffix regeneration, and the reliability of reward ranking. Those assumptions define the regime where SRD should work. In the experiments, prioritize four kinds of figures: accuracy versus token budget, direct comparisons with best-of-N and speculative rejection, reward-calibration ablations, and sensitivity analyses for boundary choice, temperature, and routing thresholds. A useful skim should take about 30–45 minutes. If reading more deeply, two follow-up questions are worth pursuing: whether boundary detection can be upgraded from interval reward scans to token-level verifier signals or hidden-state anomaly signals, and whether SRD can be composed tightly with speculative decoding, process reward models, or MCTS-style search rather than only compared against them.50:T713,PuzzleKV partitions each per-head KV cache into fixed-length logical pages and independently factorizes completed pages using low-rank decomposition. Instead of forcing the entire prompt history to share one basis, each page gets its own local basis, which better preserves region-specific directions.

The implementation has several important pieces. First, the cache is hybrid: a small sink region and a recent window are kept dense, while older completed pages are stored in factorized form. This protects the most attention-sensitive tokens from compression artifacts. Second, the attention kernel is designed to operate directly on both dense and factorized pages, so the model does not reconstruct the historical KV cache back into full space before attention. That matters for bandwidth and runtime. Third, page conversion is incremental during autoregressive decoding: once a page is filled, it becomes eligible for decomposition and storage as factors. This makes the method compatible with online generation rather than only offline post-prefill compression. Fourth, the method is training-free and calibration-free. Unlike approaches that derive a fixed compression space from model weights or calibration activations, PuzzleKV builds the representation directly from the current request's page-local KV activations.

The paper's logic is straightforward: establish that page-level low-rank structure is common across models, layers, heads, and page sizes; show that page-local bases preserve information better than a global SVD baseline; then implement the idea in a mixed dense/factorized attention pipeline that can run during decoding. The trade-off is also clear: it gives up some of the maximal sharing of a global basis in exchange for finer-grained fidelity and more stable task performance.51:T49a,Experiments are run on Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, evaluated on RULER and LongBench. The headline result is that at roughly 60% of full KV storage, PuzzleKV retains more than 96% of Full-KV performance across all tested settings. When combined with per-factor INT4 quantization, storage drops to 18.7% of the original KV footprint while still retaining more than 93% of Full-KV performance. Compared with Global SVD, PuzzleKV shows substantial gains on RULER and competitive results on LongBench.

The more informative evidence is the structural analysis. The paper shows that for page size P = 32, the effective ranks needed for accurate reconstruction vary by layer and KV head but remain well below full rank throughout the evaluated models. It also studies reconstruction quality across different page sizes and ranks, supporting the claim that page-local low-rank structure is a robust property rather than an artifact of one configuration. From a systems perspective, the results suggest that page-wise decomposition does not destroy practical decoding quality, though the paper appears more focused on quality retention than on full end-to-end serving throughput.52:T429,This is a skim paper. Start with the introduction and the main workflow figure to understand why the page is used as both the memory-management unit and the compression unit. Then read the analysis establishing page-level low-rank structure; that is the empirical premise the whole method depends on. In the method section, focus on three parts: the hybrid cache design, the mixed attention kernel over dense and factorized pages, and the incremental page conversion during decoding. Those are the pieces that determine whether the method is actually deployable. In the experiments, prioritize the comparison against Global SVD, the quality-versus-storage trade-off, and the INT4 combination results.

The paper gives strong evidence on quality retention; if throughput and latency are not equally detailed, that remains an open practical concern.53:T463,VisCache is a two-stage coarse-to-fine, training-free framework.
1) Input-stage temporal filtering: a lightweight vision-language “scout” model selects prompt-relevant keyframes before running the main VLLM. Selection uses Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) to balance query relevance and diversity, aiming to keep semantic coverage with fewer frames.
2) In-model KV pruning (PruneKV): a layer-aware visual KV compression algorithm.
- Layer-wise budget allocation: instead of uniform pruning, it uses a parabolic schedule—retain more visual tokens in early layers (fine-grained spatial details) and progressively fewer in deeper layers (more abstract semantics), evicting KV entries beyond a truncation threshold.
- Asymmetric K/V handling: keys are treated as routing/indexing signals and can be dropped more aggressively; values carry content, so values corresponding to pruned keys are fused into retained values via weighted aggregation to reduce hard information loss.
The two stages are complementary: fewer visual tokens enter the model, and the remaining visual KV footprint grows more slowly during generation.54:T582,The paper decomposes trainable state as Θ=(W, Φ, Ω): backbone weights W, normalization affine parameters Φ, and quantizer parameters Ω (scales/zero-points/rounding/rotations depending on the PTQ backend). It then runs controlled, matched-budget comparisons across these coordinate subspaces to identify where correction leverage concentrates.
SandwichQuant is a two-stage framework that only updates Φ:
1) Pre stage (SandwichQuant-Pre): train Φ_pre on the dense model to precondition response distributions presented to PTQ calibration/reconstruction. Then transfer only Φ_pre back to the original dense checkpoint and rerun the chosen PTQ backend from scratch.
2) Post stage (SandwichQuant-Post): after PTQ produces a fixed low-bit graph, freeze the quantized model and learn an independent Φ_post to correct residual response mismatch.
The separation matters: Φ_pre influences calibration/clipping/reconstruction by reshaping activations, while Φ_post targets remaining functional error after the quantized graph is fixed. The method adds no new inference modules/operators—only reuses existing norm affine parameters.
Mechanistically, the paper argues affine adaptation can fix structured response mismatch and error propagation, but cannot recover information irreversibly lost to severe clipping/rounding; gains depend on how much of the error is recoverable and aligned with the Φ subspace.55:T452,The measurements use a single NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in fp16, vLLM 0.23.0, gpu_memory_utilization=0.9, and max_model_len=32768. Increasing max_num_batched_tokens from 2048 to 32768 reduces KV capacity from about 366K tokens to about 308K tokens because roughly 3.1 GiB is reserved for prefill activations, around 16% of the KV cache. The elastic toggle remaps the full 3 GiB reserve in a few milliseconds. Static reclamation crashes under prefill bursts, so dynamic toggling is required for safety. In a low tensor-parallel, long-context setting, the dynamic scheme recovers about 18% more KV capacity and improves decode throughput by about 10% without OOM. The main negative result is stronger: a controlled TTFT-under-load experiment shows that using a smaller prefill chunk adds only about 1% median TTFT penalty. Since prefill is compute-bound and decode steps are comparatively cheap, lowering the chunk size recovers KV capacity with less machinery. Tensor parallelism further reduces the relative reserve size, from about 16% down to about 2.7% in the reported characterization.56:T5f7,The core mechanism is Expert Folding. Instead of dropping an excluded source expert or rerouting it to a similar target expert without correction, ExFold projects the source contribution onto a retained target expert. The method is motivated by two empirical findings: many experts produce directionally aligned outputs on the same inputs, but their output magnitudes differ substantially. Directional alignment makes substitution plausible; magnitude mismatch makes naive rerouting inaccurate. Based on this, each layer is calibrated with two matrices from a single frozen forward pass on unlabeled text. The scalar-projector matrix stores directed source-to-target scaling factors. The projection-loss matrix measures reconstruction loss for folding one expert into another. At inference time, retained experts are selected according to the phase budget: K_pre dominant experts per token for prefill, and D dominant experts per batch for decode. Every excluded expert is then assigned to the minimum-loss retained target, and its contribution is folded into that target by absorbing the scalar projector into the router weight. This gives one shared folding operator across both phases. Compared with token-wise sparsification, the method does not only reduce executed experts; compared with expert-set consolidation, it does not bake compression into a fixed submodel; compared with similarity-based rerouting, it explicitly corrects scale mismatch. The implementation is integrated into vLLM with a lightweight CUDA kernel.57:T4a9,The evaluation covers multiple MoE architectures and real vLLM serving workloads, focusing on TTFT, TPOT, and quality retention. The headline numbers are up to 1.41× TTFT speedup and 2.45× TPOT speedup while preserving about 99% of the original average quality. The larger decode gain is consistent with the method’s focus on reducing the active expert set under memory-bound conditions. The more informative part is the comparison structure. Against pruning or skipping baselines, ExFold degrades quality more slowly at the same budget, which supports the claim that explicit reconstruction matters. Against static merging methods, it remains adaptive to token-level or batch-level budgets instead of committing to one permanently compressed model. Against similarity-based rerouting, the directed scalar projector improves approximation when experts are aligned in direction but not in scale. The ablations indicate that both components—the loss-based target assignment and the scalar correction—are necessary. Another useful result is that the same calibrated matrices work for both prefill and decode, which reduces deployment complexity and supports the phase-unified formulation.58:T493,Hydra is a common-schema instrumentation and analysis framework. The authors instrument both HuggingFace Transformers and llama.cpp so that two very different inference stacks emit the same per-prompt timing record. The canonical schema covers at least tokenization, prefill, per-token generation, de-tokenization, inter-token latency, and end-to-end latency. These phase boundaries are then fused with high-resolution telemetry from tegrastats and NVML, enabling attribution of CPU activity, GPU utilization, DRAM traffic, power, energy, and thermal behavior to the prefill and decode windows. Two design choices matter. First, the measurement interface is decoupled from execution configuration, so models, precisions, prompt lengths, and SoC generations can be swapped without changing the analysis pipeline. Second, the framework spans both the Python framework path and the GGML/C++ path, which makes the comparison more realistic for deployment. The instantiated study covers three Jetson generations—AGX Xavier, AGX Orin, and AGX Thor—two backends, 13 instruction-tuned models from seven families, and five execution formats: bf16, F16, Q8_0, Q6_K, and Q4_K_M.59:T46b,The paper is more about stable findings than about one best number. First, performance depends jointly on backend, architecture, precision, and sequence length; model size alone is not predictive enough. Hydra’s phase-level timing shows that backend overhead, quantized decode throughput, and input/output-length scaling affect different parts of the inference pipeline. Second, quantization often reduces DRAM traffic and model footprint, but it does not automatically reduce latency or energy on edge SoCs, because CPU orchestration, GPU effective utilization, shared-memory bandwidth, DVFS, and thermal limits also matter. Third, backend choice changes CPU-side runtime behavior enough to alter decode throughput and efficiency. Fourth, gains across SoC generations are not uniformly realized; newer hardware can improve throughput or energy efficiency in some settings, but backend overheads or thermal constraints can offset part of the benefit in others. A central empirical point is that phase-aligned telemetry is necessary: aggregate latency or run-averaged power hides meaningful differences between prefill and decode.5a:T78d,The method has four stages.

1) Direction estimation. For each layer, the model collects hidden states from reflective and non-reflective examples and computes a standard mean-difference vector as an initial reflection direction. This follows the usual activation-engineering assumption that a behavior can be approximated by a linear direction in residual space.

2) Direction purification. This is the key technical step. The authors argue that the raw contrast direction mixes reflection with activation structure shared by reasoning states more broadly. They therefore apply PCA-based denoising to reduce sample noise and low-value variation, then orthogonalize the candidate reflection direction against a rank-one proxy for shared reasoning structure. A central empirical claim is that the raw direction has substantial overlap with this shared proxy, while the orthogonalized direction reduces that overlap to roughly an isotropic-random baseline.

3) Layer calibration. The method does not assume every layer is a good intervention site. On a small calibration set, it sweeps candidate layers and intervention strengths, then keeps the layers that consistently reduce reflection-like behavior without destabilizing generation quality.

4) State-dependent projection attenuation. Instead of adding or subtracting a fixed vector at every token, the method removes only the component of the current hidden state that lies along the learned reflection direction, with bounded magnitude. This makes the intervention conditional on how much reflection-associated signal is present in the current token state. Compared with constant shifts, this is a more selective suppression mechanism and is less likely to damage ordinary reasoning.

The design choice is deliberate: no retraining, no controller network, no modified decoding. The trade-off is that it needs a small reflective/non-reflective contrast set and a calibration pass.5b:T6e1,The evaluation covers three open-weight Qwen-family checkpoints on two benchmarks, MATH-500 and GPQA-Diamond, with matched answer parsing and token accounting. The main comparison is against two closely related representation-level baselines, CREST and ReflCtrl.

Across six model-benchmark settings, Reflection Steering reduces reasoning tokens by 16.9% on average while largely preserving task performance. The cleanest result is on Qwen3-30B-A3B for MATH-500: a 21.8% token reduction with only a -0.1 point change in accuracy. The paper also reports paired equivalence testing and finds support for equivalence to the raw model within a ±1 point margin, which is stronger evidence than simply reporting a small average drop.

The paper’s own framing makes clear that the strongest accuracy-preserving evidence is on mathematical reasoning. On GPQA-Diamond, the token savings remain meaningful, but the trade-off is less clean. That makes sense: in math, reflection often appears as repeated verification after the solution path is already established, whereas in scientific reasoning, revision and reconsideration may be more tightly coupled to useful inference.

The ablations that matter are: (i) raw mean-difference direction versus purified direction, showing that orthogonalization against shared reasoning structure materially improves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off; (ii) fixed vector shifts versus projection attenuation, where the latter better preserves accuracy; and (iii) layer calibration, showing that intervention quality depends strongly on depth. This is not a paper about raising benchmark accuracy. It is about recovering tokens without paying much accuracy tax, and the right way to judge it is by the cleanliness of that trade-off.5c:T6ce,The work has two layers. The first is the Thinkingbox sandbox. A task is instantiated as a finite-horizon POMDP whose latent state includes backend state, simulated-user private state, evaluator-relevant event logs, and episode status. At each turn, the agent observes dialogue history and tool outputs, then either sends a user-facing message or issues a tool call with arguments. Tool calls execute inside isolated backend sessions. The system records side effects and runs hidden executable checks at the end. A key design choice is outcome-based evaluation: multiple trajectories may be valid as long as the final backend state, required side effects, and dialogue constraints are correct.

The second layer is Thinkingbox-bench, a 507-task benchmark spanning retail/e-commerce, travel/hospitality, auto insurance, neobank internal IT support, and consulting IT/HR support. Tasks are designed around recurring enterprise patterns: lookup-then-update flows, user clarification, confirmation before irreversible actions, policy-conditioned changes, and multi-tool coordination. Most tasks are graded through executable checks over terminal backend state. An additional subset of 30 tasks uses binary rubrics on the final response, covering required disclosures, confidentiality, and consistency between what the agent says and what it actually executed.

The reliability framing is central. pass@k measures whether at least one of k attempts succeeds, which captures discovery capability. pass^k measures whether all k attempts succeed, which captures repeatable reliability. That distinction is important because many agents can occasionally find a correct trajectory while remaining unstable under sampling noise or interaction variation.5d:T56f,The main empirical result is a large discovery–reliability gap. The benchmark contains 507 tasks, and the authors evaluate 12 proprietary and open-weight models with 20 repeated trials per task. The strongest model reaches 65.36% pass@1, which is still far from dependable single-run performance. Its pass@20 rises to 91.12%, showing that many tasks are solvable at least once. But its pass^20 is only 25.25%, meaning only a quarter of tasks succeed in all 20 attempts. That gap is the central takeaway of the paper.

Because evaluation is tied to terminal backend state rather than a single final answer, the benchmark can expose failure modes that simpler tool-use benchmarks miss: updating the wrong entity, producing a convincing response while leaving the backend unchanged, missing a required side effect, introducing an extra side effect, executing high-impact actions before collecting confirmation, or generating a final message inconsistent with the actual execution outcome. The paper also includes evaluator ablations and failure analyses to show that fluent tool use is not the same as reliable work completion.

The provided excerpt does not include the full per-domain or per-model breakdown, but the headline numbers already show strong benchmark discrimination: this is neither plain function-calling nor pure dialogue evaluation; it is outcome-centric stateful execution.5e:T461,The method treats response correctness as a binary classification problem. For each query-response pair from a fixed black-box LLM, the feature set includes: (1) one or more existing uncertainty scores, and (2) neighborhood-derived features computed from a labeled reference set. The reference set is embedded, k-nearest neighbors are retrieved for each query, and statistics such as neighbor correctness and cosine similarity are added as features. A lightweight classifier is then trained to predict the probability that the current response is correct.

A key design choice is that the paper does not insist on a single learner. Instead, it compares simple classifiers and concludes that the best learner is task-dependent. This is important: the paper is not claiming a universal parametric confidence model, but a supervised calibration layer over existing UQ signals. Relative to standard zero-shot UQ, the shift is clear: uncertainty scores are treated as imperfect features, not as final confidence estimates. The neighborhood features inject local empirical risk information that zero-shot methods cannot access.5f:T42f,The evaluator state is decomposed into three typed sources: grounds for evidence, norms for decision rules, and authority for whether a rule applies to the case. For an old and revised evaluator state, each source can be taken from either version, producing a 2^3 intervention table called the judgment cube. Each hybrid state is executed through a trusted adjudicator. A source replacement set is a reason when it is sufficient to reproduce the revised verdict from the old state, and it is kept only if it is inclusion-minimal. The complete set of such minimal sufficient replacements is the judgment receipt. A key design choice is the separation between prediction and certification: a model can emit a receipt, but only execution of the counterfactual hybrids certifies it. The work also introduces paired consistency as an evaluation primitive. Control transformations carry known metamorphic relations; when a pair violates the relation, at least one prediction must be wrong. This gives an error lower bound without needing gold labels for every transformed item.60:T818,MGAL is built from long-form reports in the UN Digital Library, using position-aligned multilingual documents so that cross-lingual comparisons are not merely task-level but also semantically and structurally aligned. It covers Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian, and Spanish, with context lengths from 8K to 128K tokens. The benchmark spans four linguistic granularities—word, sentence, paragraph, and document—and includes both closed-ended and open-ended tasks. The paper mentions seven tasks in total, including word-level QA, sentence-level cloze, paragraph filling, document summarization, and translation, with 420 query-response pairs per task per language.

The key design choice is controlled stratification by evidence position. Examples are labeled by whether the relevant evidence appears at the beginning, middle, or end, indexed at both document and paragraph levels. This turns the benchmark into a diagnostic instrument rather than a generic task suite. The choice of UN reports is practical: they provide multilingual parallelism, topic consistency, and relatively regular discourse structure, which makes coherent unit definitions more reliable.

Quality control is manual and strict. The authors state that every query-response pair was audited and flawed samples were removed. This is a smaller-but-cleaner benchmark philosophy, which is appropriate for diagnostic evaluation.

Scoring is hybrid. Closed-ended tasks use precision-oriented reference metrics such as Accuracy, while open-ended tasks use ROUGE-L and, for tasks like paragraph filling where lexical overlap is insufficient, an LLM-as-a-judge setup. That trade-off is sensible: pure reference metrics under-credit semantically correct paraphrases, while pure judge-based evaluation reduces reproducibility. MGAL uses both.

Relative to LongBench, LV-Eval, M4LE, and ONERULER, the novelty is not simply broader coverage. The main difference is tighter control over variables that matter for error attribution: multilingual alignment, discourse granularity, and evidence position.61:T8dd,The experimental section is useful mainly for the error patterns it exposes. The benchmark is evaluated on 12 long-context LLMs. The main findings reported in the paper fall into four groups.

First, performance degrades as granularity becomes coarser. Models do well on word-level tasks, but performance drops at sentence, paragraph, and document levels. This suggests that many current long-context models are stronger at local matching or retrieval than at stable discourse-level integration.

Second, multilingual gaps widen in lower-resource languages. Large open-source and closed-source models are relatively comparable on higher-resource languages, but closed-source systems maintain a clearer lead on lower-resource ones, and smaller open models degrade more sharply. For pretraining, this points to data coverage and multilingual representation quality as major bottlenecks, not just architecture.

Third, position sensitivity remains strong. In sentence cloze, blanks appearing earlier in the text produce the highest error rates, with performance improving toward later positions, consistent with recency-biased attention. The authors also observe an early-option bias: models disproportionately choose earlier answer options such as A or B, indicating reliance on answer-order heuristics rather than evidence verification.

Fourth, the paper identifies two more specific failure modes. One is local semantic crowding: when neighboring sentences share entities, years, or discourse markers, models over-rely on surface overlap and pick the wrong sentence, failing to distinguish functional roles such as background, explanation, or outcome. The other is a fluency-consistency gap: generated outputs are often fluent and stylistically plausible but weakly anchored to the source, leading to factual drift and unsupported claims.

In terms of benchmark scale, MGAL covers 6 languages, 7 tasks, 4 granularities, and contexts from 8K to 128K, with 420 examples per task per language. Even without chasing a single aggregate score, this is enough to support meaningful slicing by granularity and position. The most informative numbers are likely the relative slopes across word→sentence→paragraph→document and begin→middle→end, not the overall ranking.62:T936,UpgradeBench 的设计核心是 longitudinal，而不是静态 pairwise transfer。作者沿着四代 Qwen release 加上一条 continuation release，构造了真实的升级路径；同时补充 OLMo checkpoints，因为 OLMo 的训练关系是公开且可验证的，可以把“是否来自同一训练轨迹”当成受控变量，而不是靠 release note 猜。

它把升级决策拆成四种策略：freeze、port、refresh、retrain。freeze 是继续部署旧 specialist；port 是把旧 adapter 或 task vector 直接迁到新 base；refresh 是用旧 specialist 作为 teacher，对新 base 做便宜的再专门化；retrain 则是从头按固定 recipe 重训 specialist。围绕这四种策略，作者定义并测量了几个关键量：retention、recovery cost、specialization half-life，以及 upgrade tax。这里最重要的是 retention：新策略相对“该 hop 上可达到的最佳 specialist”保留了多少收益。这样定义后，不同 hop、不同任务、不同模型规模可以放到同一坐标系里比较。

任务设置覆盖 6 个应用任务、3 类任务、2 个模型尺度，并把训练侧成本纳入 benchmark 输出，包括 GPU-minutes 和 energy。这个点做得比较扎实，因为很多迁移论文只报最终精度，不报恢复到同等质量需要多少代价，而实际部署决策恰恰取决于这个成本。

方法上它没有提出新的迁移算法，贡献在于实验设计和变量控制。尤其是对 port 的分析很关键：作者直接检验一个业界常见假设——只要新旧模型架构兼容，adapter 原样拷贝就是强基线。实验结论是否定的。决定能否直接拷贝的不是 shape compatibility，而是训练连续性，也就是两个 checkpoint 是否位于同一权重演化轨迹上，以及相距多远。

OLMo 部分进一步把这个结论做成了更接近机制层面的测量。沿同一 documented trajectory 往后走，adapter retention 会随着 continuation token 数增加而下降；文中给出的边界是，从 46B-token continuation 时仍有 0.88–0.99 retention，走到 2.9T-token continuation 时则掉到接近 no-adapter floor。后续 anneal 和 model-soup merge 并没有带来额外主要损伤。这个结果很有信息量，因为它把“能不能 port”从模糊经验变成了 distance budget 的问题。63:T8e6,实验规模不算大，但设计很完整：总共 98 次训练、193 个 evaluation cells，全部在一张 RTX 4090 上完成，并释放了 per-query prediction、bootstrap CI 和 energy log。这个设置说明作者更关心可复现的决策测量，而不是堆大算力。

几个关键结果值得记住。第一，specialist 不一定会很快过时。对于 intent classification，freeze 在 9 个 upgrade hops 上能保留 99%–101% 的 attainable gain；跨四代模型，retrained specialist 的参考分数只移动了 0.2 分，而 zero-shot 却提升了 21 分。这说明某些任务的专门化收益主要来自标签体系、输出格式或任务数据本身，base 进步并不会立刻吞掉这些收益。

第二，另一些任务则明显更依赖 base 能力。text-to-SQL 上，冻结旧 specialist 在单个 hop 上最多会损失 59% 的 attainable gain，而且它相对新 base 的优势会在三代内衰减到零。作者据此提出 data-bound 与 base-bound 的区分：前者 specialist moat 更稳，后者随着 base reasoning 能力增强会更快被追平。

第三，naive porting 可能非常危险。文中给了一个很强的反例：在两个架构完全相同但来自独立预训练运行的 checkpoint 之间，直接贴 adapter 会把 intent classification 从 92.8% 打到 42.9%，甚至低于不用 adapter 的 60.7%。但如果目标模型是同一权重继续预训练得到的 descendant，同样的操作可以保持接近 reference-level accuracy。这一组结果基本否定了“同家族同结构即可直接迁移”的经验法则。

第四，OLMo 验证复现了同样规律，并进一步定位了边界：同一训练轨迹上，随着 continuation 距离增大，port retention 从 0.88–0.99 逐步跌到 no-adapter floor；而 anneal、model soup merge 不是主要破坏源。这个结论对 checkpoint 发布和 continual pretraining 很有现实意义。

文中还给出了一个 half-life 估计：在 7–8B 规模，specialization half-life 大约落在 2–3 个 generation；在 1.5–1.8B 规模，至少观察到一次 crossing，即新 base 的便宜采用策略真正超过旧 specialist。这个量化虽然依赖任务集，但比过去泛泛讨论“要不要升级”要扎实得多。64:T955,The main design choice is longitudinal evaluation rather than static pairwise transfer. The benchmark follows four consecutive Qwen releases plus one continuation release, creating a realistic upgrade path. It also includes OLMo checkpoints, where training relationships are documented rather than inferred, allowing the authors to treat training continuity as a controlled variable.

The benchmark evaluates four upgrade strategies: freeze, port, refresh, and retrain. Freeze keeps serving the old specialist. Port copies the old adapter or task vector onto the new base. Refresh uses the old specialist as a teacher to cheaply re-specialize the new base. Retrain rebuilds the specialist from scratch under a fixed recipe. Around these strategies, the paper defines and measures retention, recovery cost, specialization half-life, and upgrade tax. Retention is especially important: it measures how much of the attainable gain on the target hop is preserved by a cheaper strategy relative to the best specialist achievable there. This makes comparisons across hops, tasks, and model scales much more meaningful.

The benchmark covers six application tasks from three classes, at two model scales, and treats training-side cost as a first-class output, including GPU-minutes and energy. That is a strong design choice because deployment decisions depend on cost-to-recover, not just final accuracy.

The paper does not introduce a new transfer algorithm. Its contribution is experimental structure and variable control. The most important analysis concerns porting. A common practitioner assumption is that if two checkpoints are shape-compatible, direct adapter copying is a strong baseline. The paper shows that this assumption is false. What licenses copying is not architectural shape but training continuity: whether the target checkpoint lies on the same weight trajectory, and how far away it is.

The OLMo experiments sharpen this into something close to a mechanistic statement. Along the same documented trajectory, adapter retention decays as continuation distance grows. The paper reports retention of 0.88–0.99 after a 46B-token continuation, but near no-adapter-floor performance after a 2.9T-token continuation. Subsequent annealing and model-soup merging add little extra damage. This turns portability from a vague family-level intuition into a distance-budget question.65:T9cb,The experimental scale is modest but well structured: 98 trainings and 193 evaluation cells, all run on a single RTX 4090, with per-query predictions, bootstrap confidence intervals, and energy logs released. The emphasis is clearly on reproducible decision measurement rather than brute-force benchmarking.

Several results stand out. First, specialists do not always become obsolete quickly. On intent classification, freezing retains 99%–101% of the attainable gain across nine upgrade hops. Over four generations, the retrained-specialist reference score moves by only 0.2 points, while zero-shot performance rises by 21 points. This suggests that some specialist value is tied mainly to task data, label taxonomies, or output conventions rather than to frontier base capability.

Second, other tasks are much more base-dependent. On text-to-SQL, the frozen specialist can forfeit up to 59% of attainable gain on a single hop, and its advantage over a newer base decays to zero within three generations. This motivates the paper’s data-bound vs base-bound distinction: some specialist moats are stable, others are rapidly eroded by improvements in the base model’s reasoning ability.

Third, naive porting can fail catastrophically. The paper gives a strong counterexample: between two architecturally identical checkpoints from independent pretraining runs, directly pasting the adapter drops intent classification from 92.8% to 42.9%, which is even worse than the 60.7% obtainable with no adapter at all. But when the target is a continued-pretraining descendant of the same weights, the same operation preserves near-reference accuracy. This directly challenges the common rule of thumb that same-family, same-shape transfer is safe.

Fourth, the OLMo validation reproduces the same pattern and localizes the boundary more precisely. Along the same training trajectory, port retention falls from 0.88–0.99 to the no-adapter floor as continuation distance increases; annealing and model-soup merge are not the main sources of damage. This is highly relevant for continual pretraining and checkpoint release strategy.

The paper also estimates a specialization half-life of roughly two to three generations at the 7–8B scale, and observes at least one actual crossing at 1.5–1.8B where cheap adoption of the new base overtakes the old specialist. The exact values are task-dependent, but this is much more concrete than the usual qualitative discussion around whether upgrades are worth it.66:T49b,Read this one with a concrete deployment or training question in mind. Start with the introduction and Figure 1, where the paper lays out the three intuitions it challenges: specialists do not always age quickly, porting is not always safe, and task differences are not well captured by a generative/discriminative split. Then read the benchmark setup and metric definitions carefully, especially retention, recovery cost, and specialization half-life. Without those definitions, the later conclusions can look like anecdotal observations.

In the experiments, prioritize the strategy comparisons across tasks and the evidence from both Qwen and OLMo supporting the claim that continuity, not architectural shape, governs portability. If you work on continual pretraining, checkpoint selection, adapter ecosystems, or practical model deployment, this is worth a full read. If you only need the main conclusions, 40–60 minutes on the main paper should be enough. The section around the independent-pretraining-run vs continued-pretraining-descendant comparison is the most important one to study closely, because it directly probes the limits of parameter-space transferability.67:T5a3,The method is an agentic LLM-as-judge setup. The data consists of pairs of revisions for the same declaration from Mathlib PRs: an earlier version that was sent back for revision, and the later version that was accepted. Importantly, each version is scored independently. The judge does not know the score of the other revision and is not explicitly told it is doing pairwise comparison, which reduces comparison leakage. The rubric decomposes proof quality into five dimensions: library leverage, automation fit, structural clarity, statement quality, and Mathlib conventions. Each dimension is scored from 1 to 10, then combined by a harness into a final score. The key design choice is tool grounding. The judge can query the exact Mathlib state at the relevant commit through bash, search for existing lemmas, inspect signatures, and check available APIs. That lets it reason like a human reviewer: is this proof reinventing something already in the library, should the statement be more general, is there a cleaner one-line invocation already available. This is materially different from a text-only judge because proof quality often depends on library context, not just the local proof text. For dataset construction, the authors used Claude Sonnet 5 to inspect historical PRs and identify cases with substantial revision differences that were not just linting or newly added declarations, then split them into development and test sets.68:T5dc,The benchmark contains 218 declaration pairs in the test split and 123 pairs in the dev split used for rubric tuning. Six judges were evaluated, including three open-weight and three closed models, with three replicates per judge. Each evaluation allows up to 20 tool calls per sample to cap inference cost. The main metric is preference alignment: whether the judge assigns a higher score to the revision that Mathlib ultimately accepted. All models perform well above the 50% random baseline. Claude Sonnet 5 is best at 80.8%, while even DeepSeek-V4-Flash reaches 63.5%, with all sign tests reported at p < 1e-5. Among open models, muse-glimmer-30b gets 70.2% and inkling-small 69.3%, showing that the task is not exclusive to frontier closed models. The most useful experimental finding is the variance analysis. Re-running the same judge on the same declarations flips roughly one-fifth to nearly half of the verdicts. Some ablations look non-significant in one replicate, p = 0.34, and significant in another, p = 0.006. That means single-run judge benchmarks can easily overstate differences. The PR 11640 case study is also informative: the initial proof reconstructed a result already present in Mathlib, while the merged revision replaced it with a one-line call to H.restrictPreimage s. The judge found the existing declaration via tool use and consistently penalized the initial version on library leverage. This kind of semantic review cannot be replicated by linting or regex heuristics.69:T6db,The reported effects are large. A model’s accuracy becomes a band rather than a point: gemma4-31b ranges from 31% to 89% on the same weights and the same items under different configurations. Across the roster, up to 85% of credited answers can be flipped to wrong by another defensible configuration. Adjacent-model rankings are not identified by stable items. Among 11 adjacent pairs, on items both models answer stably, 5 pairs are identical item by item, 4 differ on exactly one item, and the remaining 2 have disagreements that cancel to zero. Yet the full benchmark still orders every one of the 10 pairs with a nonzero full-set gap. Config-fragile items carry 95.7% of a pair’s gap on average, rising to 99.7% when pooling items rather than averaging pairs. Harness choice also changes winners: 4 of 12 models reach rank one under some configuration, and 8 of 12 reach the top three. mixtral-8x7b is 11th under the reference harness and 1st under another. The two models that win 24 of 26 configurations have median leads of 181.5 and 98.5 items out of 3,679; the other two single-configuration winners lead by only 1 and 3 items. Benchmark compression does not solve the issue. Item discrimination correlates with config-fragility at 0.28 with a 95% CI of 0.25 to 0.30, and the most discriminative items have mean fragility 0.96 versus 0.85 over the full benchmark. When compressed to 100 items, the champion count rises from 4 on the full benchmark to 5.1 for random subsets and 5.7 for discrimination-selected subsets, with a seeded tie-break range from 4 to 7. The scoring axis is especially important: holding other axes fixed, mean accuracy robust to scoring choice is 0.31, compared with 0.40 for prompt format and 0.60 for option order.6a:T74c,The core contribution is GUI-Primitives, a 994-item benchmark organized as 497 contrastive instruction pairs over seven GUI spatial primitives: left/right, above/below, containment, alignment, proximity, list ordinal, and occlusion. In each pair, the screenshot and anchor element stay fixed while the relation expression changes, so the correct target flips between two designated candidates. This minimal-pair construction is the key idea. It suppresses screenshot salience, centrality bias, and fixed-answer shortcuts: a model that always clicks the more salient element can only get one item in the pair correct.

The dataset also includes lexical variation beyond the relation term in 253 of the 497 pairs, changing verbs, head nouns, or anchor quoting, which reduces template memorization. A 196-item subset is validated by five annotators, with Fleiss kappa = 0.94 for well-formedness and kappa = 0.79 for target selection, giving the benchmark a reasonably strong annotation foundation.

Methodologically, the paper goes beyond strict point-in-box accuracy and performs candidate-level analysis. Errors are split into two types: selecting the contrastive wrong candidate versus predicting a point outside both candidate regions. This distinction matters because it changes the diagnosis. A low score does not necessarily mean the model misunderstood the relation word; it may simply have failed to localize either candidate reliably.

The paper also evaluates three training-free interventions: Set-of-Mark prompting, primitive-aware chain-of-thought, and activation steering. SoM explicitly marks the two candidates and therefore acts as an oracle upper bound on candidate discrimination rather than a deployable solution. CoT tests whether explicit reasoning helps. Activation steering tests whether internal representations can be nudged without retraining.6b:T84b,The empirical picture is consistent and fairly stark.

First, absolute performance is poor. Across 19 VLMs, the best model, Claude Opus 4.7, reaches only 31% strict point-in-box accuracy on the human-clean subset; the abstract also states that no model exceeds 32% overall. So even on tightly controlled GUI spatial primitives, current models remain far from human-level grounding.

Second, all tested models fall below the two-candidate reference level of 0.50 on four primitives: containment, occlusion, alignment, and proximity. Candidate-level analysis explains why: the dominant error is not choosing the opposite candidate, but predicting outside both candidate boxes. Depending on the model, off-candidate predictions account for 60% to 92% of errors, and on the real desktop screenshot subset this rises to 96.2%. The main bottleneck therefore looks more like candidate localization failure than relation-word confusion.

Third, the benchmark tracks downstream grounding. For the ten models also evaluated on ScreenSpot-Pro, GUI-Primitives accuracy correlates with downstream grounding accuracy at Spearman rho = +0.74 with p = 0.015. The paper also reports item-level logistic regression over n = 15,810 model-item pairs with pseudo-R^2 = 0.40, which supports the claim that the benchmark is diagnostically meaningful rather than synthetic in a disconnected way.

Fourth, only Set-of-Mark helps substantially. Marking the two candidates improves selection accuracy by 35 to 57 points, raising GPT-5 from 30% to 87% and OS-Atlas from 10% to 52%. Primitive-aware CoT and activation steering do not produce significant gains. This is a useful diagnosis: once the candidate set is made explicit, models can often discriminate between candidates much better than their raw screenshot-grounding scores suggest.

Fifth, shortcut controls behave mostly as expected. Blank canvas, shuffled instructions, and heavy blur reduce performance, indicating that the benchmark is not solved by pure template matching. The blur result is significant but not catastrophic, which suggests some models still rely on coarse visual cues.6c:T409,Its value for foundation-model research is less about the task label and more about the interface it exposes between external memory and generation. The benchmark is a clean testbed for studying why standard RAG, static memory injection, and plain chain-of-thought break when the external knowledge is procedural rather than factual. This matters for pretraining-adjacent research because future systems will likely rely on external memory that must be queried during decoding, not only on parametric knowledge. DynaRule is interesting because it turns retrieval into an internal learned process: rules are injected into KV cache, and a special token triggers step-wise re-attention and memory refresh. That is relevant to test-time memory, retrieval-trigger tokens, and training schemes that teach models to call external knowledge incrementally. The benchmark contribution feels more durable than the method itself; the method shows a clear gain, but still reads more like a strong research prototype than a settled general recipe.6d:T7e4,There are two parts: the benchmark and the model. RuleWorld contains 4.94M rules spanning four major types and seven subtypes, with both first-order logic and natural-language forms. It defines Single-Rule QA, Parallel Multi-Rule QA, and Multi-Hop Rule QA, yielding 11 sub-tasks. The benchmark design matters for three reasons. First, rules are abstract templates with placeholders, so the model must ground them before use. Second, the rule repository is shared globally rather than attached per question. Third, rules are compositional, so earlier conclusions alter what becomes relevant later.

DynaRule injects encoded external rules directly into the LLM’s KV cache and makes re-retrieval part of decoding. Rules are first embedded by a pretrained sentence encoder, then mapped into the LLM space with a lightweight adapter, and finally exposed as external memory in the KV cache. Training has two stages. In stage one, the method identifies a confidence layer, defined as the layer where attention entropy over injected rules is minimized. The intuition is that this layer exhibits the sharpest and most decisive rule selection. In stage two, the model performs Stacked Step-Level Attention Training on that layer using a special <search> token. Emitting <search> triggers re-attention over the rule memory, selects a new subset of relevant rules, and replaces outdated entries in the KV cache.

This differs from standard RAG, where retrieval is front-loaded and retrieval errors propagate through the whole generation, and from static memory injection, where the model can get stuck with early-selected rules even when later reasoning steps require different ones. Mechanistically, <search> acts like an explicit latent action: it externalizes the decision that the model needs fresh procedural support, and supervision shapes the attention pattern associated with that action. That is more interesting than adding a separate retrieval head, because it is integrated into the token-level generation trajectory.6e:T77f,The empirical message is clear: RuleWorld is hard for current strong models, especially with large rule sets and multi-step reasoning. The headline numbers reported in the paper are substantial. DynaRule improves average QA accuracy by up to 19 points across rule-injection settings, and by as much as 48 points on some sub-tasks. On retrieval, at 10K rules it achieves over 90% Recall@10 and over 85% Recall@1, beating the strongest baseline by more than 60 points.

The more important part is how the experiments are structured. The paper compares RAG-style baselines, internal injection baselines, and the proposed dynamic update mechanism. When rules are abstract and only weakly aligned with the query surface form, text retrieval becomes brittle. When tasks require parallel aggregation or multi-hop state tracking, one-shot injection degrades sharply because the relevant rule set changes across steps. Ablations show that the confidence-layer choice, the <search> token, and step-level attention training all matter. Removing dynamic re-attention or skipping step-wise supervision causes clear drops. Another useful observation is scaling behavior: as the rule repository grows, baseline performance degrades faster, while DynaRule degrades more gracefully. That suggests the gain comes from stable narrowing of attention over a large candidate set, not merely from adding extra memory.

There are also limits. The strongest results are obtained in a synthetic rule world with controlled semantics and relatively formal structure. This is enough to demonstrate feasibility for procedural knowledge use, but it is still some distance from real policy documents, noisy enterprise rules, or conflicting cross-document regulations. A second likely bottleneck is the rule encoder plus adapter. If rules become longer, noisier, or more context-dependent, the current setup may not preserve the same retrieval quality.6f:T46c,For a skim pass, start with the introduction and Figure 1 to understand why the benchmark is harder than premise-given rule QA. Then jump to the method overview and the training pipeline. Four parts deserve attention. Second, the definition of the confidence layer, because it reveals the authors’ view of where external rule selection should happen inside the network. Third, the exact role of the <search> token in re-attention and KV replacement; that is the core mechanism. Fourth, read the QA tables together with the retrieval tables, otherwise it is hard to separate retrieval failure from reasoning failure.

A useful skim should take around 20 to 30 minutes: introduction, method figure, main tables, and key ablations. If reading more carefully, two questions are worth tracking.
