And how exactly is KV replacement implemented, especially when previously selected rules may still be useful later?70:T804,The work has three main components. First, it formalizes Online Video Question Answering under Interruption. A user asks an initial question at time tq, the model starts autoregressive generation, and an interruption arrives at time ti. The observable context is the partial video V≤ti, the original question Q0, the partial answer A≤ti, and the interruption signal I. The model must jointly perform interruption-type recognition and response generation. The interruption taxonomy has three classes—Cancellation, False Trigger, and Correction—defined by whether the interruption changes the semantic context and whether it requires a change in generation strategy. That is a more meaningful decomposition than a simple stop/continue label.

Second, the paper builds OVIBench and an offline simulation protocol. The key practical challenge is reproducibility: true online interruption during generation is hard to benchmark at scale. The proposed protocol freezes a unified temporal state—what video has been seen, what has been generated, and when the interruption occurs—so models can be evaluated in a controlled and repeatable way. The benchmark supports both open-ended and multiple-choice settings. Open-ended evaluation is closer to real interaction, while multiple-choice reduces evaluation noise and makes model comparison more stable.

Third, the paper introduces a metric suite and a training set. Metrics cover interruption understanding and response generation, including interruption-intent recognition, post-interruption intent fulfillment, fluency and consistency before and after interruption, and alignment with video evidence. To test whether the benchmark can support improvement rather than only diagnosis, the authors construct OVI-Train, a multiple-choice training set for interruption-aware fine-tuning. The design choice is pragmatic: use a structured format to teach the model the chain from interruption recognition to response strategy, instead of relying only on unconstrained generation to absorb this behavior.71:T518,The main empirical result is straightforward: mainstream MLLMs that perform well on standard offline VideoQA degrade substantially under interruption. The weakest case is Correction, where the model must revise or override an ongoing answer rather than simply continue or stop. That pattern suggests the failure is not only in visual grounding, but in updating intent and rewriting generation policy mid-trajectory.

The most informative quantitative result comes from targeted fine-tuning. Starting from Qwen2.5-VL-7B, the interruption-aware fine-tuned 7B model improves multiple-choice accuracy by 16.88% and interruption-type accuracy by 13.94%, and even surpasses the 72B model in the same series. That is a strong indication that interruption handling is highly data- and objective-sensitive. Larger scale alone does not reliably induce the behavior if the model never sees the right supervision.

The paper also contrasts open-ended and multiple-choice evaluation. Open-ended testing is more realistic but noisier; multiple-choice is cleaner for controlled comparison and for closing the train-eval loop. If the benchmark is used as a diagnostic tool, the multiple-choice setting is especially useful because it helps separate failures in video understanding from failures in interruption handling.72:T664,The core idea is to replace absolute scoring of a single review with anonymized pairwise battles plus structured dimension-wise judgments. The platform has four main design choices. First, annotators are not crowd workers; they are domain experts with AI paper-writing experience. The motivation is straightforward: judging review structure, field organization, and research directions requires field-level judgment. Second, the prompts are not synthetic topics. They are derived from real, highly cited surveys so that the tasks correspond to recognizable and academically meaningful review problems. Third, the platform performs expertise matching, assigning topics to reviewers within their area, which makes the setup closer to actual peer review. Fourth, the evaluation is decomposed into five literature-review-specific dimensions: D1 literature coverage, D2 claim support, D3 paper structure, D4 research suggestions quality, and D5 overall utility.

What distinguishes this from generic arena evaluation is that the battle format is not just a scaling trick for preference collection. It is used to operationalize subjective scientific judgment in a more disciplined way. The paper also adds a second layer: using LitReviewBench as calibration data for a low-cost evaluator. The authors show that off-the-shelf LLM-as-a-judge is substantially misaligned with expert preferences and can produce incorrect system rankings. Instead of treating the judge as a drop-in replacement for experts, they explicitly supervise or calibrate it with expert preference data. That is a more careful and more useful framing for evaluator design.73:T4fe,There are four headline results. First, the benchmark contains about 3k expert judgments, each with outcomes on all five dimensions rather than only an overall preference. Second, in decisive matches against human-written drafts, even the strongest current systems achieve only a 23.0% win rate on D5 overall utility, which indicates a large remaining gap to human performance. Third, the largest deficits appear on D3 paper structure and D4 research suggestions, with models trailing humans by roughly 200 rating points. This is an important diagnosis: the bottleneck is not just retrieval or citation accuracy, but coherent field organization and non-generic research insight. Fourth, agentic systems outperform pure language models across dimensions, but they do so at a substantial inference-time cost, averaging about 15× the token budget for the same topic.

The evaluator-calibration result is also practically important. Uncalibrated LLM judges correlate poorly with expert rankings; on D5 the reported alignment is only around ρ≈0.467. After calibration using LitReviewBench, the correlation rises to about ρ≈0.792. For people working on reward modeling, evaluator design, or scalable preference supervision, this is one of the most useful findings in the paper.74:T402,Repo2Skill-Evo is built as:
1) A fixed V1 skill set produced by Repo2Skill via staged distillation plus expert refinement. Each skill is packaged (e.g., SKILL.md, optional scripts/references) and augmented with provenance metadata (source paths/symbols) to enable traceability.
2) A maintenance task: given the official V1→V2 release patch, a maintenance agent must delete or revise patch-verified obsolete skill lines while preserving still-valid content. The design intentionally emphasizes minimal, selective edits rather than full regeneration.
3) Evaluation: a strict patch-grounded headline metric that rewards correct edits on verified obsolete lines and penalizes edits elsewhere, plus a rubric-based NL judge with five dimensions for overall quality.
The analysis frames two complementary bottlenecks: incomplete localization of affected skill files (coverage) and imperfect edit selection (precision/within-file evidence tracing). An oracle localization experiment tests how much of the gap is purely localization.75:T828,KTC combines predictive uncertainty and semantic contradiction at the token level through a kernel construction, then scores that kernel with Von Neumann entropy. The intuition is straightforward. Standard token entropy only says that the model is uncertain; it does not tell whether the competing tokens correspond to equivalent phrasings or to conflicting factual content. The authors argue that the latter is much more indicative of hallucination risk.

The method has four main steps. First, at each next-token prediction step, KTC considers candidate tokens and estimates pairwise contradiction scores between them. Unlike methods such as CCP or SAR, it does not use an external NLI model. Instead, it introduces a heuristic based on neighbor-frequency statistics from Wikipedia. The idea is to use local corpus statistics to approximate whether two candidate tokens represent incompatible continuations in context. This is clearly a rougher proxy than full semantic inference, but it is extremely cheap.

Second, these contradiction relations are used to build a positive semi-definite kernel over candidate tokens, representing the semantic disagreement structure among plausible continuations. Third, KTC scales semantic uncertainty by the model’s predictive distribution. This is an important design choice: if contradictory tokens have negligible probability mass, they should not dominate the uncertainty score. The paper emphasizes that this scaling step is critical at the token level and is one of the main departures from generation-level KLE. Fourth, the normalized kernel is scored with Von Neumann entropy, and token-level scores are then aggregated to the claim level.

Methodologically, KTC sits between plain predictive entropy and heavier semantic verification pipelines. It borrows the PSD-kernel plus VNE machinery from KLE, but moves it from whole-generation uncertainty to token-level uncertainty, and replaces NLI-based contradiction detection with a corpus-statistics heuristic. The trade-off is clear: less semantic precision, much lower computational cost.76:T5e6,The evaluation uses two claim-level UQ benchmarks, MUCH and Mu-SHROOM, across four languages: English, French, German, and Spanish. The experiments cover 16 LLMs from multiple families and compare KTC against comparable white-box baselines, especially CCP and SAR.

The main empirical picture is balanced. In overall average performance, CCP remains the strongest method, while KTC ranks second with only a small gap. So KTC does not win by raw aggregate score. Its main advantage is efficiency and operating point. The paper reports at least an 8.2x speedup relative to state-of-the-art GPU-accelerated methods, while running CPU-only and requiring no extra NLI model. More importantly, KTC performs best in the high-precision regime: at recall less than or equal to 20%, it reaches 78% average precision, compared with 69% for CCP. That matters if the goal is to flag only the most suspicious claims with minimal false alarms.

The ablations also matter. The paper highlights that scaling semantic uncertainty by the predictive distribution is crucial for token-level performance; removing that step hurts results noticeably. Another practical takeaway is that the Wikipedia-based contradiction heuristic, while simple, is strong enough to serve as a useful replacement for NLI in many settings. At the same time, its limits are easy to see: it should work better for local conflicts such as numbers, entities, or short substitutions than for long-range semantic contradiction or complex entailment patterns.77:T443,For a skim read, start with the introduction and the method overview figure. The key question is whether token contradiction really captures something that plain entropy misses. Then focus on two design choices: how the Wikipedia neighbor-frequency heuristic approximates contradiction, and why semantic uncertainty must be weighted by the model’s predictive probabilities. Those are the two places where the method either stands as a coherent approach or collapses into a bag of tricks.

KTC’s case is not that it dominates average performance, but that it is much cheaper and stronger in precision-first settings. If time is limited, at least read the ablation on the scaling step. 2) Structured ground truth: Markdown for free text, LaTeX for formulas, and HTML tables for tabular content—pushing evaluation from token/character correctness toward layout/structure fidelity.
3) PDE (Prior-Driven Error): an error attribution metric intended to quantify whether a model’s mistake is better explained by language priors than by the visual evidence, capturing confident but unsupported “plausible” transcriptions.
4) Evaluation protocol: 18 contemporary MLLMs / OCR-oriented VLMs are tested under a unified setup, alongside calibrated human baselines, enabling qualitative comparison of error types (humans being conservative vs models hallucinating).79:T90d,Methodologically, this is a survey, but not a standard taxonomy survey. The authors first narrow the scope to the generative route of world models: models that map current state and action to a distribution over future observations or states. Policy-route systems are discussed as context, but not treated as simulator substitutes because their interface is fundamentally different from a state-feedback simulator. They then define an eight-capability framework: C1 asset construction, C2 physics engine, C3 interaction, C4 controllability, C5 stability, C6 state feedback, C7 diversity, and C8 evaluation metrics. This framing asks what responsibilities a model can actually assume in a simulator stack, rather than what model family it belongs to.

The main analytical innovations are threefold. First, the benchmark is external: traditional simulator capabilities, not self-referential world-model categories. That makes the gap between “looks plausible” and “simulates correctly” much easier to expose. Second, the paper uses paper-level coding to build a reproducible evidence map rather than a purely narrative review. Third, it treats state feedback as a first-class capability and quantifies it with a B1–B5 labeling scheme. This is one of the strongest parts of the paper. Many world models can emit pixels, tokens, or latent states, but they do not provide explicit object states, physical variables, queryable interfaces, or structured feedback that planners, controllers, or verifiers can reliably consume.

The paper’s overall diagnosis is also sharper than the usual “long-horizon generation is hard.” It argues that current progress is relatively stronger on interaction, controllability, and some aspects of stability, especially in short-horizon action-conditioned prediction and interactive rollouts. The structural gaps remain asset construction, physics, and state feedback. The reason is straightforward: data-driven generative models fit observation distributions well, but they do not naturally encode explicit geometry, contact dynamics, conservation laws, compositional object structure, or editable internal states. Hallucination, geometry drift, implausible collisions, and inconsistent consequences under identical actions are all treated as symptoms of missing invariants.7a:T624,This is not an experimental methods paper; its empirical contribution is a corpus audit. The most important quantitative facts are these. First, the study builds a curated corpus of about 200 papers and performs systematic coding on 163 implementation papers. Second, Section IV-F conducts a paper-level audit of state-feedback interfaces and quantifies them with a B1–B5 scale, leading to the conclusion that state feedback is both essential for simulation and structurally absent in much of the literature. Third, after comparing progress across the eight capabilities, the paper concludes that controllability, interaction, and parts of stability are relative strengths, while asset construction, physics engines, and state feedback remain clear weaknesses.

The most useful “results” are not single benchmark numbers but the uneven capability profile. Many systems are already competent at visual realism, short-horizon rollouts, and action-conditioned generation. Performance degrades quickly when the requirement shifts to long-term consistency, explicit physics, object-level state, or verifiable feedback. The paper repeatedly grounds this diagnosis in recurring failure modes: objects appearing or disappearing without cause, geometric drift over long rollouts, contact and collision behavior that violates physical intuition, and inconsistent outcomes under the same action. For pretraining researchers, these failure patterns are more informative than a single leaderboard score because they point directly to weaknesses in objectives and representations.7b:T4ad,For a quick read, focus on three parts. Start with the Introduction and Figure 1 to understand why the paper insists on simulator capabilities rather than model taxonomies. Finally, read Section IV-F carefully, including the B1–B5 labeling scheme. That is the most original analytical component.

If you only have 30–45 minutes, read in this order: Introduction, capability definitions, the main summary figure/table, Section IV-F, then the future directions. It helps to read the paper as a requirements document for simulator-grade world models rather than as a literature catalog. Two issues are worth deeper follow-up. One is the paper’s claim that hallucination is a consequence of conditional sampling rather than physical solving; that has implications for diffusion-based video models, autoregressive video models, and JEPA-style predictive learning alike. The other is the absence of state feedback, which directly limits the use of world models as environments for planning, RL, and tool-using agents.7c:T7c5,The contribution is a benchmark and execution environment rather than a new model. The paper defines a mobile planner as the high-level decision core of an on-device assistant: it interprets user intent, retrieves long-term memory, invokes structured business APIs, loads reusable composite skills, and delegates specialized subtasks to GUI sub-agents when direct tool use is insufficient. Around this setup, the benchmark is organized into four capability dimensions. Basic Tool Use covers utility calls, multimodal input handling, strict execution order, permission boundaries, and OS feedback. Sub-agent Collaboration measures whether the planner can decompose tasks and hand them off to downstream specialists with valid context transfer. Memory Usage tests whether the agent can retrieve persistent user context—preferences, credentials, prior state—to resolve underspecified requests before planning. Skill Usage evaluates whether the planner can invoke packaged multi-step skills instead of replanning every primitive action, reducing long-horizon error accumulation.

Operationally, MobilePA-Bench runs in an executable sandbox with live application databases and structured feedback. The key design choice is to decouple central planning from low-level visual parsing. In other words, the benchmark is intentionally not centered on pixel understanding; it is centered on deciding when to call an API, when to query memory, when to invoke a composite skill, and when to fall back to a GUI sub-agent. This keeps the evaluation focused on planner quality rather than visual noise, while still preserving realistic friction such as call dependencies, permission blocks, and dynamic state mutations.

The benchmark itself contains 1,705 real-world tasks across 13 domains and 212 tools. The task design aims at realistic workflows, such as multi-day travel planning, where success depends on cross-tool coordination and state-aware execution rather than single-step tool selection.7d:T4f3,The main empirical message is that current strong LLMs still struggle in this interactive, stateful, tool-centric mobile setting. The best model reaches only 75.52% overall, which is a useful signal: the benchmark is not saturated, and realistic mobile planning remains far from solved under the paper’s task formulation.

The failure analysis is more informative than the headline score. The paper highlights four recurring weaknesses: errors under strict tool-call ordering, weak recovery from runtime system exceptions, unreliable memory retrieval for ambiguous user requests, and brittle coordination across multiple agents or execution modes. These are not superficial UI failures; they point to deficits in closed-loop planning under constraints.

In terms of scale, 1,705 tasks over 13 domains and 212 tools are large enough to support capability-level slicing. The excerpt does not expose the full per-model table, but the paper’s emphasis is clear: the benchmark differentiates models mainly through dynamic constraints and interaction feedback, not through static API matching. When reading the experiments, the useful question is not who ranks first, but where errors accumulate along the chain of planning, tool invocation, state update, and recovery.7e:T465,This is a skim paper. Start with the introduction and make sure the critique of existing function-calling and GUI benchmarks is clear; that critique explains every major design decision. That is where the paper’s evaluation target becomes precise.

Next, inspect the sandbox design: live databases, structured feedback, permission blocks, and dynamic state mutation. If time is limited, 30–40 minutes is enough. If you want to reuse ideas for agent training environments or RL-style evaluation loops, revisit the task schema and feedback interface more carefully.7f:T75d,POOL is a wrapper around any per-query confidence estimator. Let the base estimator M be verbal confidence, a sampling-based diversity score, or a hybrid. POOL does not modify M internally. Instead, it embeds query stems with a fixed encoder, builds semantic neighborhoods in embedding space, and forms overlapping clusters. For each cluster, it selects a medoid and runs the expensive base estimator only on that representative. The resulting score is treated as a cluster-level confidence signal. For an individual query, POOL then aggregates the scores propagated from all clusters it belongs to, using soft similarity-based weighting, to produce a query-specific confidence estimate.

Two design choices matter. First, clusters are overlapping rather than disjoint. This lets a query borrow evidence from multiple local neighborhoods and reduces dependence on a single clustering decision. Second, POOL introduces a rescue budget. If the propagated scores for a query disagree strongly across its clusters, the method spends extra budget on that query to reduce variance and improve reliability. In effect, computation is concentrated on hard or unstable cases instead of being spread uniformly across the batch.

The paper also introduces a simple hybrid baseline, Hy@p, combining verbal confidence with sampling-based diversity. This is a sensible move: propagation only helps if the base signal is reasonably informative. A stronger per-query estimator gives POOL a better foundation for amortization.

Conceptually, POOL is an inference-time meta-algorithm rather than a new uncertainty theory. Its success depends on two assumptions: semantic redundancy exists in the batch, and embedding-space proximity correlates with similarity in correctness patterns, not just topical similarity. The rescue mechanism is the paper’s practical answer to violations of these assumptions.80:T53e,The experiments cover multiple base estimators, several domains, and five black-box LLMs. The paper compares verbal confidence, spectral sample-diversity confidence, and the proposed hybrid Hy@p. Among the per-query baselines, Hy@5 achieves the best average AUROC across five datasets and five black-box models.

Using Hy@5 as the base estimator, POOL retains 93.5% to 97.9% of the unpooled AUROC while reducing confidence-estimation generations by 39.3%, 29.3%, and 19.3% under different rescue budgets. This is the main empirical result: most of the ranking quality is preserved while a meaningful fraction of generation cost is removed.

The paraphrase-augmented setting is especially informative. When the workload is enriched with semantically redundant queries, savings rise to 73%–76%. That makes the operating regime of the method very clear: POOL works best when the batch contains repeated semantic structure. If queries are highly heterogeneous and independent, the room for amortization shrinks.

The right way to read the results is through the trade-off curve, not a single AUROC number. The paper is not claiming a universally better uncertainty signal. It is showing that strong but expensive black-box confidence estimators can be shared across semantic neighborhoods instead of being paid for independently on every query.81:T42a,This is a skim-to-medium-depth paper. Start with the introduction and lock in the problem definition: black-box confidence ranking, not white-box calibration. Then go straight to the method overview and notation. The key pieces are overlapping clustering, medoid evaluation, soft propagation, and the rescue budget. Once those four steps are clear, the method is essentially understood.

In the experiments, first inspect the comparison among base estimators to see why Hy@5 is used as the main foundation. Then read the AUROC retention versus generation savings results for POOL against the unpooled baseline. Finally, pay attention to the paraphrase-augmented workload, because it reveals the main boundary condition of the method: it relies on exploitable semantic redundancy.

If time is limited, 25–35 minutes is enough. If you care about large-scale evaluation, black-box routing, or confidence monitoring in production, spend extra time on the rescue-budget design, overlap strategy, and embedding choice, since those details will determine practical gains.82:T793,The paper has two main components. First is CorrGap, a metric for inter-dimension dependence. Instead of measuring only the overall correlation between judge scores and human scores on a target dimension, CorrGap asks whether the judge becomes less accurate exactly on examples where the target dimension differs strongly from the other dimensions. The authors convert human scores within each dimension into percentiles, which avoids artifacts from different score distributions across dimensions. For each text and target dimension, they compute the gap between the target-dimension percentile and the mean percentile of the non-target dimensions. Small-gap examples form a low-variance group; large-gap examples form a high-variance group. If the judge evaluates the target dimension independently, its correlation with human labels should be similar across the two groups. If it leaks information from non-target dimensions, the high-variance group should suffer more, because those are precisely the cases where dimensions disagree. CorrGap is defined from this correlation difference, with additional care to control for target-score distribution so that the metric does not simply reflect example difficulty.

The second component is DimCheck, an inference-time intervention over chain-of-thought. The judge first produces reasoning for the target dimension. A checking step then identifies evidence in that reasoning that is unrelated to the target dimension, such as comments about fluency when scoring factuality. Those irrelevant pieces are iteratively removed, and the model re-evaluates the text conditioned on the cleaned reasoning. The key idea is to constrain the evidence basis of the score, rather than only changing the instruction prompt. The paper also explores using smaller models to approximate the larger-model checking component, which is important because the method otherwise adds nontrivial inference overhead.83:T4c7,The main contribution is the dataset and evaluation protocol. The authors start from protocol versions modified by scientists on Benchling and compare them against published source protocols. The observed differences are converted into first-person scientist queries and weighted rubrics. A correct answer is expected not only to propose the modification itself, but also to address downstream implications. The benchmark contains 149 tasks derived from 96 published protocols across nine wet-lab biology domains. Each task is reviewed by at least two independent scientists with a relevant PhD and at least three years of bench experience. Review criteria include question relevance, scientific soundness, rubric reasoning depth, rubric scientific accuracy, and overall quality; only high-quality tasks are retained. During evaluation, models receive the query, the source protocol, and internet access, and produce a free-form answer. Scoring is done with an LLM judge that evaluates each rubric criterion separately on a 0/1/2 scale, then aggregates with criterion weights into a normalized score. The paper also reports grader-consistency checks and intentionally uses a coarse scoring scale to improve judge stability.84:T442,Nine models are evaluated, including Claude Opus 5, the GPT-5.6 family, Gemini 3.6 Flash, Grok 4.5, Kimi K3, GLM 5.2, and Inkling. Each task is attempted ten times. Invalid outputs, such as formatting failures or refusals, are assigned zero and tracked separately. Models are given the query, the published protocol, and web access; proprietary models use their native search tools, while open models use Exa. Performance is reported as a normalized weighted-rubric score between 0 and 1. From the available text, the paper emphasizes benchmark quality and evaluation protocol more than headline model gaps. The key empirical points are: (1) tasks come from real protocol modifications rather than synthetic expert-authored prompts, (2) scoring is criterion-wise and weighted, which makes open-ended evaluation more structured, and (3) grader agreement was checked across representative judge models. For exact model rankings and breakdowns by intent or biology domain, the tables and appendices would need to be consulted, since the provided text does not include the full numeric results.85:T60e,The method has three pieces. First, a formalization: evaluator validity is represented as a pair (S, R), not a single scalar. The paper argues and proves that the two coordinates are independent, and that R is not interpretable without S, because a noisy judge can appear responsive for the wrong reasons. This motivates a validity frontier instead of one-number ranking. Second, an intervention design around scientific overclaiming. The authors define scope edits that widen the set of situations a claim covers—broader populations, adjacent domains, stronger quantifiers, turning an observation into a standing property. They define strength edits that keep scope fixed but increase commitment—removing conditions, deleting hedges, adding unsupported intensifiers. Edit direction is set by human annotators rather than inferred from model outputs. Third, a measurement and validation protocol. They evaluate 7 judges across 4 domains, separately scoring invariance and sensitivity, and separately analyzing scope versus strength. They also introduce validation power, which asks whether a dataset forces the evaluator to rely on the construct rather than on provenance or surface cues. A key point is the distinction between item mode and paired mode: only paired minimal-edit evaluation can expose sensitivity failures that are invisible in ordinary per-item scoring. The paper also revisits the earlier finding that prompting for accuracy worsens overgeneralization, and shows that the effect differs by axis, resolving the apparent paradox.86:T4a2,Three empirical findings stand out. First, the measured profiles show that several judges are not terrible on invariance but are weak on construct sensitivity, and the weakness is asymmetric. Judges tend to react more to strength edits than to scope edits, suggesting that they are better at detecting stronger-sounding certainty than at noticing semantic expansion of applicability. Second, the replication of accuracy pressure reveals opposite movement on the two axes, which explains why earlier work could observe more overgeneralization under an 'accuracy' prompt. Third, the validation-power analysis on 5 public datasets shows a large gap between item mode and paired mode. The same datasets can look acceptable when scored item by item, yet only about 55%–67% of the relevant signal is recoverable in paired form, indicating substantial leakage from generation conditions or other shortcuts. This also reconciles two seemingly conflicting observations mentioned in the introduction: negligible verbosity bias in a large audit versus a calibration set where length alone predicts labels better than the judge. The issue can lie in the label construction, not only in the judge.87:T46b,The main contribution is the twin-prefix framework. Starting from a gold plan, the authors inject one environment-accepted error at a fixed slot to create a bad prefix, and keep an otherwise identical clean twin differing in exactly that one write. Around the same anchor slot, they render five nested review prefixes with lengths L in {1, 2, 3, 5, 8}. This keeps error type, error position, goal, and executed context fixed, making review length the only manipulated variable. Evaluation is centered on Youden informedness, J = catch - false rejection, which prevents reject-everything behavior from looking good. They also report score-mode AUC with per-length recalibration, so score distributions at different lengths are compared fairly. A subtle but important design choice is that longer windows follow batch deployment semantics: actions inside the reviewed window are not yet executed, so their observations are unavailable. The paper later isolates this observation-deprivation channel with a replay intervention. The work also tests whether any label-blind deployment policy can outperform a calibrated fixed short unit.88:T6e6,The core method is residual-guided non-parametric optimization. The system starts from a fixed base verifier and iteratively improves it around observed mistakes. At each round, the current verifier is replayed on a construction pool, and disagreements with labels are collected as residuals. Recurring residual patterns are then abstracted into rule cards. Each card records a missing verifier bias together with support examples, counterexamples, applicability conditions, and abstention conditions. This is a key design choice: instead of directly updating model parameters, the method converts recurring failure modes into explicit knowledge units.

A rule card can follow one of two promotion paths. If the missing bias can be expressed as deterministic comparison logic—such as numerical tolerance handling, unit normalization, scientific notation conversion, or specific symbolic equivalence rules—it goes through code audit and replay validation, and if accepted becomes a code module. A code module is a deterministic verifier unit that returns Correct, Incorrect, or Abstain. If the bias cannot be fully codified and still requires model judgment, it is incorporated into the fallback verifier prompt rather than compiled into code. At inference time, the system first runs the module library; cases that can be decided explicitly are handled there, and only unresolved cases are sent to a fixed model-based fallback verifier.

What distinguishes this from prior work is not simply adding tools, but turning verifier improvement into a closed loop: residual discovery, rule-card drafting, replay validation, and promotion into either executable modules or prompt guidance. It sits between hand-maintained rule libraries and opaque judge-model behavior.89:T545,The paper evaluates on four reference-based verification benchmarks. The headline result is 93.05% macro accuracy, outperforming the reported rule-based, model-based, scientific, and tool-augmented baselines included in the study. The more informative result is the component ablation: compared with a prompt-only setting, adding code modules yields an additional +1.76 macro-accuracy gain. That suggests the benefit is not merely better prompting; explicit comparison logic is covering verifier blind spots that prompting alone does not fix. In addition, direct module decisions reduce fallback model calls by 32.13%, so the system improves both accuracy and inference efficiency.

The experiments are most convincing when read as evidence for two claims. First, recurring residuals do contain reusable verifier biases that can be extracted. Second, splitting those biases into deterministic modules versus prompt-level guidance works better than relying on a single prompt-only or model-only verifier. A careful reader should still pay attention to the relationship between the construction pool and the evaluation benchmarks: if they are too similar, rule extraction becomes easier. The replay-validation protocol, support/counterexample design, and cross-benchmark consistency are therefore important for judging how robust the method really is.8a:T462,For a quick read, start with the motivating examples in the introduction, especially the discussion of when 1+3.14 should or should not be treated as equivalent to 1+π. Controlled interventions in Appendix L show that changing an omitted semantic coordinate can change the conclusion even with fixed observations and predictions.95:T736,The method, NAPE, starts from a log-mel spectrogram, splits it into non-overlapping patches, and projects each patch into a latent embedding. This yields a 2D grid of patch embeddings. Since the backbone is a causal Transformer over a 1D sequence, the grid must be serialized with a scanning order. The model then predicts the embedding of the next patch from the prefix, using a lightweight predictor head. Training uses negative cosine similarity to a stop-gradient target embedding, rather than L2 regression or classification over discrete acoustic tokens.

The most interesting technical point is that scanning order is treated as a first-class design choice. In images, rasterization is often a convenience. In audio spectrograms, time and frequency axes play very different roles, so the serialization order changes both the available causal context and the inductive bias. The paper studies four scanning strategies and shows that this choice materially affects transfer performance and training behavior. The trade-off is intuitive: if the order destroys temporal continuity, the model no longer follows natural acoustic evolution; if it only marches along time, it may underuse local time-frequency structure. Making this axis explicit is one of the paper’s main contributions.

Architecturally, the setup is deliberately minimal: a single causal encoder plus a predictor head, with no teacher branch, no EMA target network, no reconstruction decoder, and no extra variance/covariance regularization. This is the key difference from much of prior audio SSL. The model is not trained to reconstruct masked content or to match a teacher representation. It is trained to model audio as a sequential latent process, which makes it much closer in spirit to language modeling and easier to align with unified multimodal pretraining recipes.96:T5a7,Pretraining is done on AudioSet, with downstream evaluation on ESC-50, Speech Commands V1/V2, and IEMOCAP. The paper reports three model sizes: Small (19M), Base (85M), and Large (303M), mainly to test whether the objective scales. According to the full text, NAPE reaches state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art performance on several tasks, and importantly it also performs well under linear probing, not just full fine-tuning. That matters because next-embedding prediction does not explicitly optimize for linear separability.

The ablations are more informative than the headline numbers. The paper studies scanning order, model scale, and objective/architecture choices. The main takeaways are that scanning order matters a lot, temporally aligned serialization is usually stronger and more stable, and performance improves consistently from Small to Large without obvious breakdown of the objective. The fact that this works without a decoder, tokenizer, or teacher is itself an empirical result. The qualitative analyses, including attention maps and embedding-space structure, suggest that the model captures meaningful acoustic boundaries and local spectro-temporal patterns. If the goal is to assess relevance for unified multimodal pretraining, spend extra time on the serialization design and the cosine latent-prediction loss, because those are the pieces most likely to transfer to broader next-latent frameworks.98:T9bd,Libra 的核心设计是 decoupled vision-language system：一套 vision system，一套 language system，中间用 cross-modal bridges 连接。关键不只是双塔，而是在每层内部把 self-modal modeling 和 cross-modal interaction 分成两种计算模式。

第一是 switch attention。作者区分两种场景：模态内部建模时，用标准 attention；跨模态交互时，不直接让一种模态去对齐另一种模态的原始特征空间，而是先通过 cross-modal bridge 把 Q/K/V 映射到新的交互空间，再做注意力。这么做的动机很明确：如果直接共享同一注意力空间，视觉和语言会互相拉扯，尤其在数据不平衡时更容易让弱势模态被强势模态同化。bridge 相当于给跨模态交互加了一个受控接口，保留各自表示的自治性。

第二是 switch FFN。它对应不同任务场景下的后续变换分流，用来进一步区分理解与生成、以及自模态与跨模态信息融合后的处理方式。虽然从摘要和引言看，具体实现细节需要结合方法章节确认，但设计意图很清楚：attention 负责信息路由，FFN 负责场景化变换，二者共同完成“共享框架下的计算解耦”。

在实例化上，作者给了两个版本。Libra-1 面向 understanding-only image-to-text。这里有两个值得注意的点：一是 supervision 采用 unified discrete autoregression，把视觉和语言都放进离散 AR 框架里，优先换取训练稳定性；二是 vision input 采用 hybrid tokenization，把连续视觉信号和离散 ID 结合起来，试图兼顾细粒度感知与离散序列训练的稳定性。这个选择说明作者并不完全相信纯离散视觉 token 足够表达感知细节。

Libra-2 扩展到 unified understanding + generation。按引言描述，它在 tokenization、representation、supervision 上又加了额外策略，目标是同时支持 image-to-text 和 text-to-image。这里最关键的不是“能不能统一”，而是统一后是否还能维持两边能力不互相伤害。Libra 的回答是通过结构分流降低干扰，而不是完全依赖数据配比去硬平衡。

如果和典型 unified MLLM 比，Libra 的区别在于它不把跨模态交互视为默认状态，而把它视为一种需要显式开关和专门映射空间的计算模式；如果和 cascade 比，它又没有把视觉生成完全外包给独立大后端，而是保留了端到端联合学习的可能。99:Ta8b,Libra is a decoupled vision-language system with one vision branch and one language branch connected by cross-modal bridges. The key idea is not merely having two towers, but introducing two computation modes inside the model: self-modal modeling and cross-modal interaction.

The first component is switch attention. For self-modal modeling, Libra uses standard attention. For cross-modal interaction, it does not directly align one modality into the raw feature space of the other. Instead, queries, keys, and values are mapped through a cross-modal bridge into a dedicated interaction space before attention is computed. The motivation is clear: direct sharing of the same attention space can cause one modality, usually language, to dominate the other under imbalanced data. The bridge acts as a controlled interface that preserves modality-specific representations while still allowing information exchange.

The second component is switch FFN. It further separates computation after attention depending on the scenario, helping distinguish self-modal processing from cross-modal fusion, and likely also understanding from generation. The exact implementation details need the method section, but the design intent is straightforward: attention handles routing, FFN handles scenario-specific transformation, and together they realize decoupled computation within a unified framework.

The paper instantiates the framework in two versions. Libra-1 targets understanding-only image-to-text modeling. Two details matter here. First, supervision uses unified discrete autoregression over both vision and language, prioritizing training stability. Second, vision inputs use hybrid tokenization, combining continuous visual signals with discrete IDs to balance fine-grained perception and stable sequence modeling. This suggests the authors do not fully trust purely discrete visual tokens to carry enough perceptual detail.

Libra-2 extends the framework to joint multimodal understanding and generation. According to the introduction, it adds further strategies in tokenization, representation, and supervision to support both image-to-text and text-to-image. The central claim is not simply that these tasks can be unified, but that they can be unified without one side damaging the other, thanks to structural decoupling rather than only careful data balancing.

Compared with typical unified MLLMs, Libra treats cross-modal interaction as an explicit computation mode with dedicated mappings, not as the default state of every layer. Compared with cascade systems, it does not outsource visual generation to a separate large backend, so it preserves the possibility of end-to-end joint learning.9a:T597,From the available full-text fragment, the experiments are organized in two settings: Libra-1 for multimodal understanding and Libra-2 for joint understanding and generation. Third, whether this decoupled design still holds at much larger data scale, or mainly serves as a practical compromise under current multimodal data limitations.9c:T753,The paper introduces VGAU-Diag, a fine-grained evaluation framework for vision generation-assisted understanding. The framework has three main components. First, it performs difficulty-aware evaluation by stratifying samples rather than collapsing everything into one aggregate score. This is meant to reveal whether visual generation helps consistently or only on easier cases. Second, it supports controlled comparison across three representative paradigms under the same setting: Vision-CoT, where textual and visual reasoning are interleaved; Generate-then-Answer, where the model first creates auxiliary visual content and then reasons in text; and Vision-Reasoning, where the visual output itself serves as the reasoning product. Third, it introduces Oracle-Assisted Reference Protocols that decouple generation quality from understanding ability by supplying faithful or controlled visual aids.

The task domain is visual planning. Models must infer task-relevant spatial states from images and produce executable action sequences. This is a useful choice because it is verifiable and exposes a clearer causal chain between visual state estimation and final decision quality than standard multiple-choice benchmarks. The paper also revisits prior Vision-CoT evaluations and argues that some gains were inflated by optimal-step prior leakage, meaning the model could benefit from structural priors rather than from the actual generated visual content. After correcting for that issue, targeted Generate-then-Answer becomes more reliable than generic stepwise visual reasoning.

This is fundamentally an evaluation paper. Its value lies in decomposing the broad claim that generation helps understanding into measurable sub-questions: Is the generated visual aid relevant? Is it faithful? Can the model use it? Does the benefit persist as reasoning difficulty increases?9d:T643,The empirical findings are organized around diagnosis rather than leaderboard performance. First, the benefit of visual generation is strongly difficulty-dependent. It can help on easier instances, but the gains become unstable as reasoning complexity increases. Second, oracle-assisted analysis suggests that visual understanding is often the dominant bottleneck. Even when faithful visual aids are provided, current unified multimodal models may still fail to exploit them effectively. In contrast, stronger proprietary VLMs benefit more from oracle aids, which indicates that the limitation is not only generation quality.

Third, the paper identifies a three-stage transition in generation-assisted understanding. Task-irrelevant visuals mostly act as interference. Visually plausible but incorrect aids can actively mislead the model. Only high-fidelity, task-aligned visual aids provide stable assistance. Fourth, after removing prior leakage in earlier Vision-CoT-style evaluations, a more targeted Generate-then-Answer strategy is more reliable than generic visual step-by-step reasoning. The implication is that useful visual generation should focus on decision-critical states rather than simply adding more intermediate visual outputs.

1) Image–text entropy: from layer k, obtain visual tokens and text tokens; compute a prompt-relevant distribution via temperature-scaled softmax over CLIP similarities, then compute Shannon entropy H_S = -\sum p\log(p+\epsilon). High entropy indicates dispersed attention, consistent with fragmented or noisy prompt-relevant regions.
2) ECS (Entropy-based Cropping Strategy, inference): evaluate a small set of candidate crops/aspect ratios; compute H_S using very early layers (k=1 in ECS) and pick the crop with minimal entropy; combine the selected crop with the original image as the final input.
3) ERT (Entropy Regularization Training, fine-tuning): add entropy as a regularizer to the standard next-token loss: L = L_NTP + \alpha H_S (k=2 in ERT). The paper argues this sharpens attention on relevant tokens (p_i > 1/e) while suppressing irrelevant ones (p_i < 1/e), loosely analogous to negative-sample suppression in contrastive learning. Implementation is LoRA-based with only ~0.14% trainable parameters.9f:T6cd,The method has two layers. First, a diagnostic framework. In each trajectory, the agent retrieves candidate pages, inspects page images, writes source-linked findings into working memory, and finally outputs both a final answer and terminal memory. A frozen reader then sees only the question plus terminal memory and produces a memory-only answer. An official judge scores both the final answer and the memory-only answer against the gold answer, yielding binary indicators for answer correctness and memory answerability. This produces a four-cell analysis, with special attention to P_mmc, the fraction of answer-correct cases whose terminal memory is still not answerable. The key design choice is that memory quality is defined functionally—whether it preserves enough information for answering—rather than stylistically.

Second, the training algorithm AWM-GRPO. All compared agent variants share the same Qwen3-VL-4B policy, retrieval harness, tools, memory schema, prompts, and optimizer; only post-training and reward differ. For each sampled trajectory, the policy emits a final answer and terminal memory; the frozen reader answers from memory alone; the judge scores both outputs. GRPO then ranks trajectories using not only final-answer correctness but also memory-only answerability, preferring trajectories that both solve the task and leave behind answerable memory. This differs from answer-only GRPO, which optimizes the end result but is indifferent to the quality of the stored state. The input to this stage is a per-frame spatial grid of visual features, preserving a 27x27 token layout instead of flattening everything into a 1D sequence upfront. The method has three main ingredients. First, the fast-weight parameterization is convolutional rather than MLP-based. Unlike TTT-MLP or SSM-style operators such as Mamba that process flattened sequences, the hidden state here is represented by two grouped convolution kernels, W1 and W2, which together define a time-varying convolutional mapping over the 2D feature grid. Grouping partitions channels into subsets, allowing specialization while keeping the update efficient. Second, the module uses causal inner-loop updates. For each frame, lightweight heads produce keys, values, queries, per-group learning-rate gates, and momentum coefficients. These signals drive gradient-style updates to the fast weights, and the updated convolutional mapping contextualizes the current stream using only preceding history. The causality claim is specifically about update ordering: each frame can only depend on accumulated past state, not future frames. Third, the model uses a hybrid frame selector. Instead of training an auxiliary scoring network, it derives change-aware importance directly from the inner-loop training signals, combining gradient-direction shifts and alignment-loss deltas with uniform sampling. This is meant to preserve both scene transitions and within-scene changes under a fixed frame budget. The full pipeline processes videos in chunks with state carried across chunk boundaries, normalizes importance after the full pass, selects a fixed number of frames, and then applies the original MLP projector to map selected visual features into the LLM embedding space.a3:T5d6,The strongest part of the empirical section is the controlled comparison setup. GoT-R1-1B first emits a textual plan containing object spans, attributes, and bounding boxes, then generates 576 image tokens conditioned on both prompt and plan. The analysis has four parts. First, metric validation: the authors swap the two boxes inside the model's own chain, creating a known layout corruption, and test whether different evaluators detect it. Second, decoder-faithfulness tests: they compare planned relations against detected image layouts, and perturb object-segment order or remove the chain to identify what signal the decoder actually uses. Third, external-plan injection: they feed oracle plans into the decoder while varying text style and box statistics, to test whether execution depends on planner-specific phrasing, likelihood, or simply geometric quality. Fourth, inference-time repair: they apply symbolic verification, resampling, and minimal edits to planner outputs without retraining the model. Another important negative result is that removing the chain sharply hurts object presence, indicating that the plan is a primary conditioning channel rather than a decorative explanation layer.a6:T8b0,方法叫 Reward-based Velocity Matching，简称 RVM。核心做法很直接：先用当前模型生成 endpoint 样本 x0，根据 reward model 或任务奖励给每个样本一个标量回报；然后把 x0 前向加噪到某个中间时刻 xt，并构造该时刻对应的 velocity target v；最后不再估计 policy ratio，也不再回放整条反向去噪轨迹，而是直接用 reward 变换得到的权重，对 velocity prediction 做带符号的回归更新。

直观上，正奖励样本会强化与该样本对应的 velocity 方向，负奖励样本会抑制它。作者还引入了 anchor velocity v_anc，作为独立于 reward 的稳定器。anchor 可以来自参考模型、原模型或其他保守目标，用来约束模型不要因为奖励优化而快速漂移，避免画质、语义对齐或运动先验被破坏。这样，RVM 的设计空间被压缩成三个真正重要的维度：reward 如何映射成权重；anchor 如何选；样本如何 rollout 生成。

论文的一个理论贡献是统一视角。作者指出，近期一些看似不同的方法，如 RAM 和 DiffusionNFT，在特定 reward 设计和 anchor 选择下都可以写成 RVM 的特例。这个统一很有价值，因为它说明争论焦点不该放在损失公式表面长什么样，而应放在更实质的地方：奖励信号质量、权重变换是否稳定、anchor 强度如何影响保真与偏移、以及 rollout sampler 的成本与偏差。

另一个关键点是 trajectory-free。传统 trajectory-based 方法需要存储随机去噪路径上的中间状态，并把最终奖励分配回这些随机转移，训练成本高且方差大。RVM 只需要 endpoint 样本，再独立采样一个噪声时刻做单步 velocity matching，因此可以和 deterministic ODE sampling 结合，显著降低 rollout 成本。作者还强调不需要 classifier-free guidance，这进一步减少了训练和采样开销。

从方法定位看，这不是 diffusion pretraining，而是 post-training。但它和 pretrain 的接口很紧：更新目标直接沿用 velocity matching 这一原生训练表征，而不是强行套用 AR policy gradient 语言。这种接口设计是全文最有启发的部分。a7:T82c,The proposed method is Reward-based Velocity Matching (RVM). The procedure is simple. First, generate endpoint samples x0 from the current model and score them with a reward function. Then forward-noise each x0 to an intermediate state xt, construct the corresponding velocity target v, and update the model by regressing its predicted velocity toward or away from that target using reward-derived signed weights. Positive rewards reinforce the velocity direction associated with a sample; negative rewards suppress it.

A key ingredient is the anchor velocity, v_anc. This acts as an independent stabilizer and can be derived from a reference model or another conservative target. The anchor is meant to control drift and preserve desirable properties such as visual quality, semantic alignment, or motion priors while still allowing reward-driven adaptation. Under this view, the real design choices are not hidden in a policy-ratio derivation. They are explicit: how to transform rewards into weights, how to choose the anchor, and how to generate samples.

The paper also provides a unifying lens. It shows that recent methods such as RAM and DiffusionNFT can be recovered as special cases of RVM under particular reward and anchor choices. That is useful because it shifts attention away from superficial differences in loss algebra and toward the substantive issues: reward quality, stability of weighting schemes, anchoring strength, and rollout efficiency.

Another important property is that RVM is trajectory-free. It does not require storing the full reverse denoising path or assigning terminal rewards back through stochastic transitions. Instead, it works from endpoint samples plus independently noised intermediate states. This makes it compatible with deterministic ODE sampling and avoids some of the variance and systems overhead of trajectory-based approaches. The method is post-training rather than pretraining, but its strongest idea is precisely at the pretrain/post-train interface: adapt the model in the same representation space in which it was originally trained.a8:T6e9,The experiments cover three settings: text-to-image with Stable Diffusion 3.5, text-to-video with Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, and image-to-video with SkyReels-I2V. The main empirical claim is that trajectory-independent, velocity-based methods consistently match or outperform trajectory-based baselines while being substantially cheaper to train.

The clearest efficiency result is on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B. The RVM recipe uses a 16-step deterministic ODE rollout without classifier-free guidance, yet achieves better performance at much lower training cost than trajectory-based methods such as DanceGRPO and FlowGRPO. The exact table values are not fully visible in the provided text, but the systems implication is clear: in video generation, removing trajectory storage and stochastic reverse-path dependence is a major practical gain.

A particularly important finding concerns reward design. Standard preference and visual-quality rewards can improve benchmark scores while pushing the model toward nearly static videos. The paper identifies this as a failure mode of the reward, not necessarily of the optimization rule. To address it, the authors introduce a dynamic-tracking (DT) reward based on optical flow, explicitly encouraging meaningful motion. Adding DT substantially improves VBench Dynamic Degree and also raises the overall VBench score. This is one of the most useful takeaways in the paper: reward specification may matter more than increasingly complicated policy-loss design.

When reading the experiments, pay special attention to three comparisons: trajectory-based versus ELBO-based versus RVM in cost and quality; ablations over reward-to-weight mappings and anchor choices; and the motion-quality trade-off before and after adding DT reward in video tasks.a9:T4a4,Start with the Introduction and the first part of the method section. A time-dependent vector field vθ transports a simple prior p1, usually noise, to the data distribution p0 through an ODE. Standard training fits the conditional velocity along interpolation paths. FlowDPO-style methods avoid exact likelihood computation by replacing log probabilities with timestep-wise flow regression errors, then applying a DPO-like pairwise objective to winner and loser samples. The paper shows why this can be unsafe: the preference update can alter the terminal endpoint of the flow in directions that are normal to the pretrained data manifold. Optimal flow matching recovers the terminal data distribution, but a preference update leaves the manifold whenever its induced terminal displacement has a nonzero normal component. ThermoDPO addresses this by adding a temperature-controlled winner-side anchor. As the temperature τ goes to zero, the objective recovers rejection sampling fine-tuning. For τ>0, it decomposes into a temperature-scaled FlowDPO term plus a nonnegative anchoring term. This makes the alignment–preservation trade-off explicit. The weighted variant, ThermoDPO-weighted, fixes practical weighting issues near t=0 and comes with a bound on a reconstruction-based surrogate for manifold drift.ab:T858,方法叫 R²-OPD，关键设计有三步。第一步，用 teacher-independent 的 process reward 估计 reasoning progress。做法不是只看最终答对与否，而是对连续推理状态采样后续 continuation，比较从不同中间状态继续生成时的 solve probability 变化，把某段推理对最终解题概率的边际贡献当作 progress signal。作者强调 raw process reward 噪声很大，原因一是 Monte Carlo continuation 采样方差，二是中间 reasoning span 的边界本身不稳定。

第二步，做 sign-consistent span merging。原始轨迹先被切成 reasoning spans，然后把 process reward 符号一致、相邻的 span 合并成更大的 segment。这样做有两个目的：一是减少对细粒度边界估计的依赖，二是让后续比较发生在更稳定的语义单元上。文中给了理论说明：如果内部边界估计有误差，合并后这些误差在段内会相互抵消；同时对 token-level divergence 做段内平均，也能在弱相关假设下降低局部方差。

第三步，用 ranking conflict 做 reward filtering，而不是 reward replacement。对每个合并后的 segment，作者聚合 token-level reverse-KL distillation loss，得到该段“偏离 teacher 的惩罚强度”；同时用 process reward 给出该段“推进解题的贡献”。如果两个排序冲突，例如 progress 更高的段反而被蒸馏损失惩罚得更重，就说明 teacher guidance 在这一局部可能不可靠。R²-OPD 不把 process reward 加到 loss 里，也不重写 OPD objective，而是把这些冲突段的 distillation reward mask 掉，只保留 progress 与 distillation 一致的部分继续监督。这个选择很关键：它把 process reward 用作校验器而不是训练主信号，降低了高噪声 reward 直接驱动优化的风险。

从实现上，论文基于 reverse-KL OPD，并采用 support-restricted 近似来计算 token-level KL，只在学生或师生联合的 top-H support 上做分布匹配，避免全词表计算。R²-OPD 叠加在这个标准 OPD 框架之上，因此兼容现有 on-policy 蒸馏流水线。ac:T866,The method, R²-OPD, has three main components. First, it estimates reasoning progress using teacher-independent process rewards. Instead of relying only on final correctness, it samples continuations from successive intermediate reasoning states and measures how the probability of solving the task changes. This gives a marginal contribution estimate for each reasoning span. The paper emphasizes that raw process rewards are noisy because continuation-based estimation has Monte Carlo variance and because fine-grained reasoning boundaries are themselves unstable.

Second, it performs sign-consistent span merging. The trajectory is segmented into reasoning spans, and adjacent spans with process rewards of the same sign are merged into larger segments. This reduces sensitivity to noisy internal boundaries and creates more stable units for calibration. The theoretical discussion argues that internal boundary estimation errors can cancel within merged segments, and that averaging token-level divergence over a segment reduces local variance under weak dependence assumptions.

Third, it detects local ranking conflicts between progress and distillation penalty, and uses those conflicts for filtering. For each merged segment, token-level reverse-KL distillation losses are aggregated into a segment-level penalty for deviating from the teacher. Process reward gives a segment-level estimate of reasoning advancement. If a higher-progress segment is penalized more heavily than a lower-progress one, the two signals disagree in ranking, indicating that teacher supervision may be unreliable there. Instead of adding process reward into the objective or replacing OPD, R²-OPD masks distillation rewards on the most inconsistent segments and keeps teacher guidance elsewhere.

This design choice is the core idea. Process reward is treated as a reliability probe rather than a primary training signal, which avoids directly optimizing against a high-variance reward. The implementation is built on reverse-KL OPD with support-restricted approximation over a top-H token set, so the method can be layered onto standard practical OPD pipelines.ad:T776,The experimental section is aimed at validating the signal-calibration hypothesis rather than demonstrating a large-scale model jump. The tasks are reasoning-heavy, and the comparisons include vanilla OPD, variants that directly incorporate outcome or process rewards, and alternative filtering or weighting strategies.

Three findings stand out. First, the mismatch is real: the paper provides qualitative examples and aggregate analysis showing that some intermediate spans increase downstream solve probability while receiving stronger distillation penalties because they diverge from the teacher distribution. This is especially visible on harder reasoning problems.

Second, the gains come from removing bad supervision rather than injecting another reward. Compared with directly mixing process rewards into optimization, the filtering-based approach is more stable and more consistently helpful. The explanation is straightforward: raw process rewards are noisy, so using them as direct optimization targets can distort learning, whereas using them only to suppress clearly inconsistent teacher signals is safer.

Third, the ablations support the two main design choices: sign-consistent merging and segment-level averaging. Without merging, conflict detection becomes more brittle because boundary noise leaks into the comparison. With token-level filtering instead of segment-level filtering, lexical fluctuations create more false conflicts. The paper also studies the masking ratio and shows that more masking is not always better; excessive filtering removes useful teacher transfer.

1) Image-to-dataset retrieval: given an image v, retrieve Top-K similar image-text pairs R_v from a paired corpus D using an image retrieval model.
2) CRS (Caption Refinement Suggester): extract semantic elements that consistently appear across the retrieved captions; these act as “must-preserve / should-include” anchors.
3) CQA (Caption Quality Assessor): use the generated caption as a query to retrieve another set R_c; discrepancies between R_v and R_c are interpreted as hallucinations (caption introduces content that shifts retrieval away from the image-based neighborhood) or omissions (missing details that prevent alignment).
4) RL training uses CRS+CQA outputs to guide caption refinement, encouraging generation of new candidates rather than merely scoring existing ones.
Key differences vs common RL captioning: it avoids relying on a single VLM/CLIP scalar judge, does not require extra keyword annotations, and aims to reduce reward hacking by grounding feedback in retrieval-set consistency—assuming the retrieval model and corpus are reliable.b0:T485,The framework, Multi-Turn Certified Robustness (MTCR), models conversation as a State-Adversarial MDP. Dialogue history is mapped to a continuous state; at each turn an adversary chooses a user message from an epsilon-bounded perturbation set; the LLM responds according to its policy; and the state is updated. Safety is defined by a predicate over the state space. The central quantity is k-turn certified robustness: the worst-case probability of staying safe for k turns under any adaptive adversary. A naive certificate gives a lower bound of p^k, where p is the worst-case single-turn certified safety probability. MTCR tightens this through embedding-space mode decomposition, separately certifying intra-mode safety and inter-mode transitions. It also introduces (alpha, beta)-safety persistence, a structural condition under which the degradation can improve from p^k to beta^k when beta is larger than the worst-case single-turn bound, with a linear characterization 1 - k(1 - beta) for interpretable horizon estimates. The paper also discusses tightness for non-overlapping decompositions and impossibility results without structural assumptions.b1:T49c,The dataset contains 40 Korean conference sessions, 19 medical and 21 finance, with multilingual segments preserved when present. The paper compares several training routes. One is direct decision-token SFT, which tends to produce a stronger classifier but suppresses reasoning. Another is a masked objective that preserves the model’s native reasoning, but only on cases the model already solves correctly; this means it receives little useful signal on failure cases and therefore struggles to improve beyond the base reasoning policy. The authors point out a key limitation of group-relative RL objectives: when all sampled rollouts agree, there is no learning signal, even if they all agree on the wrong answer. That leaves many confidently wrong prompts untouched. For auditing, the paper combines activation probes with behavioral interventions. Probes test when the decision becomes decodable in the hidden states, while interventions remove or replace parts of the generated reasoning to see whether the final action changes, which is a more causal test of whether reasoning matters. The adapter is not simply turned on or off. Its strength is scaled continuously inside the model, with the effective transformation written as h' = (W + gΔW)h. This makes the method closer to interpolation between the base model and a safety-adapted model, rather than hard switching or post-hoc filtering.

A key design choice is that the gate is trained jointly with the safety adapter. It is not an external moderation classifier. The gate directly modulates internal computation during generation. The paper defines safety alignment narrowly as post-training interventions such as safety-focused SFT, RLHF, or DPO, and excludes earlier-stage mechanisms like harmful-data filtering. This setup is stronger than the usual decoupled protocol where safety is measured on harmful prompts and utility on unrelated benign tasks. Standard benign tasks often do not activate safety filters at all, so they mostly capture broad side effects of alignment rather than the cost of active safety mechanisms. By contrast, over-refusal prompts are designed to engage safety behavior while remaining safe enough that helpfulness is still a meaningful target.

Still, the paper presents the effect as systematic rather than anecdotal, and it explicitly notes that current multilingual safety training does not remove the disparity.ba:T66e,The method is a two-stage Diagnose-and-Generate loop. In the first stage, Diagnose & Allocate, the system estimates the effective supervision yield of the current practice distribution: given the current student and a set of prompts, how likely is it that sampled rollouts will contain both correct and incorrect trajectories, producing a usable preference pair? Rather than making topic-level decisions from raw counts, DIAG uses Empirical Bayes shrinkage to stabilize estimates under low sample counts. This prevents overreacting to noisy topics that happen to look good or bad due to small numbers. It also allocates budget between exploration and exploitation, so the curriculum does not collapse too early onto a narrow subset of topics.

In the second stage, the teacher generates follow-up problems conditioned on the student’s recent mistakes. This is the key departure from standard active learning. Instead of selecting uncertain prompts from a static candidate pool, DIAG actively creates new prompts that target the student’s current failure modes. The paper also uses uncertainty-weighted resampling to concentrate compute near the competence boundary rather than spreading it uniformly.

Conceptually, the method optimizes two quantities at once: pair yield and pair quality. Pair yield determines how much supervision is available per unit budget. Pair quality determines whether preference learning happens on examples that are actually informative for the current student. Compared with brute-force scaling of rollout width, DIAG tries to increase the probability that each sampled problem produces useful contrastive signal.bb:T5af,From the provided full-text content, the experimental emphasis is not on a single benchmark headline but on showing that DIAG produces more informative preference pairs under the same or lower budget, and converts that higher signal density into better mathematical reasoning performance. The method uses no safety training data, no reference policy, and adds no inference overhead.be:Ta1d,方法叫 BPCO（Best-Practice Critic Optimization）。它由五个关键部件组成。

第一，用 DPPO 替代标准 PPO clipping。标准 PPO 用概率比值裁剪，低概率 token 的微小绝对变化也可能触发 clipping，而高概率 token 可以承受更大的绝对变化；在大词表 LM 中，这会让不同 token 的更新几何很不均匀。DPPO 把约束改成 sampled token 概率的绝对变化上界，相当于让每个被采样 token 共享同一 absolute-probability trust region，更适合语言模型的长尾词分布。

第二，把 critic 输出限制在 reward range 内。论文考虑的是 outcome reward，回报天然有已知范围。若 value head 仍是无界线性层，训练早期很容易出现超范围预测，随后 GAE 和 value loss 都会被放大。作者将 value prediction bounded 到 reward 支持集，使 critic 的函数类与任务先验一致，减少无意义外推。

第三，critic 直接拟合 Monte Carlo return，而不是常见的 bootstrap target。由于中间 reward 全为 0、终局才给分，且 γ=1 的设置很常见，此时用 bootstrap target 的收益并不大，却会把旧 critic 的误差传播到新 critic。BPCO 直接用观测到的最终回报训练 value，相当于在 outcome-only 场景里主动放弃一部分低方差，换取更少偏差和更稳定的 critic 学习。

第四，policy update 不做 batch-wise advantage normalization。作者的论点很直接：当策略逐渐收敛时，真实 advantage 的尺度本来就应该变小；若每个 batch 都强行归一到单位方差，就等于持续放大残余噪声，容易造成后期训练抖动甚至过更新。BPCO 保留 raw advantage scale，让优化器看到“信号正在衰减”这件事。

第五，使用 length-adaptive GAE。固定 λ 在短回答和长回答上对应的 terminal reward 传播形状不同，导致 credit assignment 随长度系统性偏移。作者设计按 response length 调整的 λ，使不同长度样本上终局奖励向前传播的权重分布更一致。

除此之外，论文还强调一个 critic-only 的额外自由度：privileged critic input。因为 critic 只在训练时使用，可以额外看到 reward-defining information，例如数学题参考答案、官方解、或开放式任务的 rubric，而 policy 仍只看原始 prompt。这样不会改变最优 value function 的定义，但会显著降低 value approximation 难度。这个点和传统 RLHF/GRPO 的差别很大：group-relative estimator 很难自然利用这类只在训练时可见的信息。bf:T7b2,实验分三层。

第一层是 controlled sanity test。作者构造了一个小而可解的数据设定，用“能否稳定拟合”来隔离优化问题，而不是把失败归因于任务难度。这里最有信息量的结论是：bounded value head、MC target、去掉 advantage normalization、以及 length-adaptive GAE 都能单独改善稳定性；把这些组件叠加后，critic baseline 从容易发散或震荡，变成可持续下降并收敛的训练曲线。这个部分更像训练病理分析，建议认真看。

第二层是数学推理主实验。数据规模是 40.3K problems，并在两个 30B-A3B 的 MoE 模型上评估。文章的主张不是“critic 远超 group-based RL”，而是更克制：BPCO 相比原始 critic baseline 在不同模型和数据规模上都更稳、更强；同时在只用每个 prompt 一个 response 的条件下，性能可以追平或超过 group-based baseline。这里真正重要的是 sample efficiency 叙事：GRPO 需要每 prompt 多条 rollout 才能形成组内相对优势，而 BPCO 用单条 rollout 就能构造 token-level advantage。

第三层是 privileged information 实验，包括数学任务里给 critic 参考答案，以及 rubric-reward 任务里给 critic rubric。结果显示 privileged input 往往能加快 critic 学习，但对最终 policy 的收益并不总是单调增加；当 critic 过拟合训练分布时，value 更准不一定转化成更好的 policy improvement。这个观察很重要，因为它提醒人们：critic 监督更强，不等于 actor 更新一定更好，关键还要看 value error 的分布是否与 policy improvement 方向一致。

从摘要和正文可确认的硬数字包括：40.3K 数学数据集、两个 30B-A3B MoE 模型、single-rollout 设置对比 group-based baseline。若做复现，建议重点记录各 ablation 对 value loss、KL、reward variance、以及训练后期稳定性的影响，而不只看最终 pass@1。c0:T95d,The proposed recipe is BPCO, Best-Practice Critic Optimization. It combines five design choices.

First, it replaces standard PPO clipping with DPPO. Standard PPO clips the probability ratio, which means low-probability sampled tokens can be clipped by tiny absolute probability changes while high-probability tokens tolerate much larger ones. In large-vocabulary language models, this creates uneven update geometry. DPPO instead clips the absolute probability change of the sampled token, giving a common absolute-probability trust region.

Second, it bounds value predictions to the reward range. In outcome-reward settings, the return support is known. An unconstrained linear value head can easily overshoot that range, especially early in training, which then destabilizes both value fitting and downstream advantage estimates. Bounding the value head injects a simple but strong task prior.

Third, it trains the critic on Monte Carlo returns rather than bootstrapped targets. Because intermediate rewards are zero and the terminal reward carries the whole signal, the variance reduction from bootstrapping is limited while the bias from critic self-reinforcement can be severe. BPCO therefore prefers direct supervision from observed outcomes.

Fourth, it removes batch-wise advantage normalization in the policy update. The argument is that as the policy improves, the residual advantage scale should naturally shrink. Forcing every batch to unit scale erases that information and can keep magnifying noise late in training. BPCO preserves the raw advantage magnitude.

Fifth, it introduces length-adaptive GAE. With a fixed lambda, terminal reward is propagated backward with a length-dependent profile, so short and long responses receive systematically different credit assignment. The adaptive schedule is designed to make the effective weighting of terminal reward more consistent across response lengths.

A notable extra feature is privileged critic input. Since the critic is discarded at inference time, it can condition on reward-defining information unavailable to the policy, such as a reference answer, official solution, or grading rubric. This does not change the ideal value function for a prompt, but it can make that function much easier to approximate. That is a meaningful advantage over group-relative estimators, which do not naturally exploit such side information.c1:T650,The empirical section has three layers.

The first is a controlled sanity test on a small solvable setup. This is arguably the most informative part of the paper because it isolates optimization pathologies from task difficulty. The ablations show that bounded value prediction, Monte Carlo targets, removing advantage normalization, and length-adaptive GAE each improve stability, and their combination turns a fragile critic baseline into a trainable one.

The second layer is the main mathematical reasoning evaluation on a 40.3K-problem dataset, using two 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts models. The claim is measured rather than inflated: BPCO consistently improves over the critic baseline across scales, and with only one rollout per prompt it matches or exceeds a group-based baseline. The key point is sample efficiency and token-level credit assignment, not merely final accuracy.

The third layer studies privileged information. In math, the critic can see a reference answer; in a rubric-reward task, it can see the grading rubric. This often accelerates critic learning, but the policy gain is task-dependent and can weaken when the critic overfits. That is a useful result: a more accurate critic is not automatically a more useful critic for policy improvement.

The hard numbers explicitly stated in the paper include the 40.3K math dataset, two 30B-A3B MoE models, and single-rollout comparisons against group-based training. For reproduction, the most important metrics to track are not just final reward or accuracy, but also value loss behavior, KL, reward variance, and late-stage training stability.c2:T45c,Start with the introduction, because the paper frames instability as a set of mismatches rather than a vague implementation issue.
